# =============================================================================
# FORMAT-AGNOSTIC HELPER FUNCTIONS
# These functions work seamlessly for both Word and PDF output
# =============================================================================

# Add significance stars (plain text - works in both formats)
add_stars <- function(p) {
  stars <- as.character(symnum(p, corr = FALSE, na = "", cutpoints = c(0, .001, .01, .05, 1),
         symbols = c("***", "**", "*", "")))
  stars
}

# Format term labels using Unicode (works in both Word and PDF)
pretty_diag_term <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("group", "Diagnosis: ", x)
  x <- gsub("Diagnosis: 1", "Diagnosis: BPD", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Diagnosis: 2", "Diagnosis: AD", x, fixed = TRUE)
  # Use Unicode × instead of LaTeX $\times$
  replacements <- c(
    "Diagnosis: BPD:round" = "Diagnosis: BPD × round",
    "Diagnosis: AD:round" = "Diagnosis: AD × round",
    "Diagnosis: BPD:round_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × round_c",
    "Diagnosis: AD:round_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × round_c",
    "Diagnosis: BPD:lag_net_return" = "Diagnosis: BPD × lag_net_return",
    "Diagnosis: AD:lag_net_return" = "Diagnosis: AD × lag_net_return",
    "Diagnosis: BPD:investment_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × investment_c",
    "Diagnosis: AD:investment_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × investment_c",
    "round_c:investment_c" = "round_c × investment_c",
    "Diagnosis: BPD:round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × round_c × lag_net_return_c",
    "Diagnosis: AD:round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × round_c × lag_net_return_c",
    "round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "round_c × lag_net_return_c"
  )
  for (i in seq_along(replacements)) {
    x <- gsub(names(replacements)[i], replacements[i], x, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  # Replace remaining colons with × for interaction terms
  x <- gsub(":", " × ", x)
  x
}

clean_tactical_term <- function(term) {
  term <- dplyr::recode(term,
                        "(Intercept)" = "(Intercept)",
                        "lag_fair_gap_sc" = "Fairness gap (t-1, z)",
                        "prev_stake_sc" = "Previous stake (z)",
                        "prev_invest_sc" = "Previous investment (z)",
                        "curr_invest_sc" = "Current investment (z)",
                        "ns(round, df = 2)1" = "Round spline 1",
                        "ns(round, df = 2)2" = "Round spline 2",
                        .default = term)
  pretty_diag_term(term)
}

format_pval <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  formatted <- ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    NA_character_,
    ifelse(x < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), round(x, digits)))
  )
  # Remove leading zero for p-values (APA style)
  sub("^0\\.", ".", formatted)
}

format_pval_clause <- function(x, digits = 3, fallback = "= n/a") {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    fallback,
    ifelse(x < 0.001, "< .001", paste0("= ", format_pval(x, digits = digits)))
  )
}

# Format p-value columns in a data frame (pipe-friendly)
format_p_cols <- function(df) {
  # Find columns that look like p-values
  p_cols <- grep("(?i)^p$|^p[\\._-]?val|^Pr\\(|p-value", names(df), perl = TRUE)
  for (col in p_cols) {
    if (is.numeric(df[[col]])) {
      df[[col]] <- format_pval(df[[col]])
    }
  }
  df
}

# =============================================================================
# FLEXTABLE-BASED TABLE FUNCTIONS
# These create APA-style tables that work in both Word and PDF
# With proper cross-referencing support for bookdown
# =============================================================================

# Main APA-style table function using flextable
# @param df Data frame to display
# @param caption Table caption text (without label markup)
# @param label Cross-reference label (e.g., "my-table" -> \@ref(tab:my-table))
# @param note Optional footnote
# @param bold_sig Whether to bold significant p-values
# @param font_size Font size (default 10)
apa_flex <- function(df, caption = NULL, label = NULL, note = NULL,
                     bold_sig = TRUE, p_col = NULL, alpha = 0.05,
                     font_size = 10) {

  # Identify p-value columns if bold_sig is requested
  if (bold_sig && is.null(p_col)) {
    p_col <- grep("(?i)^p$|^p[\\._-]?val|^Pr\\(", names(df), perl = TRUE)
  }

  ft <- flextable::flextable(df) |>
    flextable::theme_apa() |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = font_size, part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1)

  # Bold significant p-values
  if (bold_sig && length(p_col) > 0) {
    for (col_idx in p_col) {
      col_name <- names(df)[col_idx]
      p_vals <- df[[col_name]]
      if (is.character(p_vals)) {
        num_vals <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9\\.eE-]", "", p_vals)))
        sig_rows <- which(!is.na(num_vals) & num_vals < alpha | grepl("^<", p_vals))
      } else {
        sig_rows <- which(!is.na(p_vals) & p_vals < alpha)
      }
      if (length(sig_rows) > 0) {
        ft <- flextable::bold(ft, i = sig_rows, j = col_idx)
      }
    }
  }

  # Add cross-referenceable caption
  if (!is.null(caption)) {
    if (!is.null(label)) {
      if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
        ft <- flextable::set_caption(ft, caption = caption)
      } else {
        # Use officer::run_autonum for Word output (avoids duplicate LaTeX labels)
        ft <- flextable::set_caption(
          ft,
          caption = flextable::as_paragraph(
            flextable::as_chunk(caption)
          ),
          autonum = officer::run_autonum(
            seq_id = "tab",
            bkm = label,
            pre_label = "Table ",
            post_label = ": "
          )
        )
      }
    } else {
      # No label - just add plain caption
      ft <- flextable::set_caption(ft, caption = caption)
    }
  }

  # Add footnote if provided
  if (!is.null(note)) {
    ft <- flextable::add_footer_lines(ft, values = note)
    ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = font_size - 1, part = "footer")
    ft <- flextable::italic(ft, part = "footer")
  }

  ft
}

# Wrapper for supplement tables (simpler styling)
supp_apa <- function(df, caption = NULL, label = NULL, note = NULL, font_size = 9) {
  ft <- apa_flex(df, caption = caption, label = label, note = note, font_size = font_size)

  ft <- flextable::set_table_properties(
    ft,
    layout = "autofit",
    width = 1,
    align = "center"
  )

  # The LaTeX writer emits the stored column widths and adds \tabcolsep
  # (2 pt) on both sides of every column, so the stored widths must fit
  # inside the 6.5 in text width minus that padding. Cell text wraps.
  usable_width <- 6.5 - ncol(df) * 4 / 72.27
  column_widths <- dim(ft)$widths
  if (sum(column_widths) > usable_width) {
    ft <- flextable::width(
      ft,
      width = column_widths * usable_width / sum(column_widths)
    )
  }

  flextable::set_table_properties(
    ft,
    layout = "fixed",
    width = 1,
    align = "center",
    # A table continued across pages must not repeat its caption, because
    # the repeated caption defines the cross-reference label a second time.
    opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)
  )
}

# Final fitting step for supplement tables whose chunks set column widths by
# hand: shrink the widths proportionally if they exceed the text width minus
# LaTeX cell padding, and stop captions repeating on continued pages.
supp_fit <- function(ft, max_width = 6.5) {
  column_widths <- dim(ft)$widths
  usable_width <- max_width - length(column_widths) * 4 / 72.27
  if (sum(column_widths) > usable_width) {
    ft <- flextable::width(
      ft,
      width = column_widths * usable_width / sum(column_widths)
    )
  }
  flextable::set_table_properties(
    ft,
    layout = "fixed",
    width = 1,
    align = "center",
    opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)
  )
}

# Legacy wrapper for compatibility
legacy_apa_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, note = NULL, ...) {
  apa_flex(df, caption = caption, note = note)
}

# Read the merged data if it's not already in R environment
full_dat <- read.csv("Data/full_RTG_data.csv")

# Filter out missing group labels and exclude ASPD (small n; not analyzed)
full_dat <- full_dat[!is.na(full_dat$group), ]
full_dat <- full_dat[full_dat$group != "ASPD", ]

nrow(full_dat)  # Should be 13,290 if 1329 games * 10 rounds

# Document attrition: Count initial subjects by group and role
initial_counts <- full_dat %>%
  distinct(subject_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  count(group, role, name = "n_initial")

# Check round distribution
table(full_dat$round)

round_counts <- full_dat %>%
  count(subject_ID, round) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = round, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# Look for subjects with != 1 in any round
problematic_subjects <- round_counts %>%
  filter(if_any(-subject_ID, ~ .x != 1))

# Document which subjects are being excluded and why
excluded_subjects <- full_dat %>%
  semi_join(problematic_subjects, by = "subject_ID") %>%
  distinct(subject_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  dplyr::select(subject_ID, group, role)

# Count exclusions by group and role
exclusion_counts <- excluded_subjects %>%
  count(group, role, name = "n_excluded")

print(problematic_subjects)

# Remove problematic subjects from the dataset
full_dat <- full_dat %>%
  anti_join(problematic_subjects, by = "subject_ID")

# Count final subjects by group and role
final_counts <- full_dat %>%
  distinct(subject_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  count(group, role, name = "n_final")

# Create attrition summary table
attrition_summary <- initial_counts %>%
  left_join(exclusion_counts, by = c("group", "role")) %>%
  left_join(final_counts, by = c("group", "role")) %>%
  mutate(
    n_excluded = replace_na(n_excluded, 0),
    n_final = replace_na(n_final, 0)
  ) %>%
  arrange(role, group)

# Total attrition across all groups
total_attrition <- tibble(
  n_initial_total = sum(attrition_summary$n_initial),
  n_excluded_total = sum(attrition_summary$n_excluded),
  n_final_total = sum(attrition_summary$n_final),
  percent_excluded = round(100 * sum(attrition_summary$n_excluded) / sum(attrition_summary$n_initial), 1)
)

attrition_group_summary <- attrition_summary %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_initial = sum(n_initial),
    n_excluded = sum(n_excluded),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(n_included = n_initial - n_excluded)

attrition_group_matrix <- cbind(
  excluded = dplyr::pull(attrition_group_summary, n_excluded),
  included = dplyr::pull(attrition_group_summary, n_included)
)
rownames(attrition_group_matrix) <- dplyr::pull(attrition_group_summary, group)

attrition_group_test <- fisher.test(attrition_group_matrix)
attrition_group_test_name <- "Fisher's exact test"
attrition_group_p <- format_pval_clause(attrition_group_test$p.value)

# Recreate game_id with clean data

  group_by(subject_ID) %>%

# Create contrasts and tactical-event flags used across analyses
clean_dat <- full_dat %>%
  arrange(subject_ID, round) %>%
  group_by(subject_ID) %>%
  mutate(
    return_0 = if_else(is.na(return_ratio) & investment == 0, 0, return_ratio),
    # Fair return definition: amount that equalizes investor/trustee payoffs
    # For investment >= 5: fair_return = 2*investment - 10
    # For investment < 5: fair_return = 0 (since 3*investment < 10, any positive return exceeds fairness)
    # This threshold reflects the tripling mechanism: investor sends x, trustee gets 3x
    # Investor has (20-x) + return; Trustee has (3x - return)
    # Equal payoffs: 20 - x + return = 3x - return => return = 2x - 10
    # NOTE: For investments < 5, this convention means any positive return is "better than fair"
    # This may inflate responsiveness opportunities; consider alternative definitions if needed
    fair_return = if_else(investment >= 5, 2 * investment - 10, 0),
    better_than_fair = return > fair_return,
    worse_than_fair = return < fair_return,
    lag_investment = lag(investment),
    lag_return = lag(return),
    lag_better_than_fair = lag(better_than_fair),
    lag_worse_than_fair = lag(worse_than_fair),
    investor_responsiveness_event = case_when(
      role != "investor" ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(lag_better_than_fair) ~ NA_real_,
      !lag_better_than_fair ~ NA_real_,
      investment > lag_investment ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    investor_retaliation_event = case_when(
      role != "investor" ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(lag_worse_than_fair) ~ NA_real_,
      !lag_worse_than_fair ~ NA_real_,
      investment < lag_investment ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    trustee_coaxing_event = case_when(
      role != "trustee" ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(investment) | investment <= 0 ~ NA_real_,
      investment > 5 ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(return) ~ NA_real_,
      return >= investment ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    trustee_encouragement_event = case_when(
      role != "trustee" ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(lag_investment) | is.na(lag_return) ~ NA_real_,
      investment >= lag_investment ~ NA_real_,
      return > lag_return ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    trustee_coop_pickup_event = case_when(
      role != "trustee" ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(lag_investment) | is.na(lag_return) ~ NA_real_,
      investment <= lag_investment ~ NA_real_,
      return > lag_return ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    fair_gap = return - fair_return,
    lag_fair_gap = lag(fair_gap),
    # Headroom + change indicators capture whether investors can move up/down
    headroom_up = if_else(role == "investor" & !is.na(lag_investment), as.numeric(lag_investment < 20), NA_real_),
    headroom_down = if_else(role == "investor" & !is.na(lag_investment), as.numeric(lag_investment > 0), NA_real_),
    investor_increase = if_else(role == "investor" & !is.na(lag_investment), as.numeric(investment > lag_investment), NA_real_),
    investor_decrease = if_else(role == "investor" & !is.na(lag_investment), as.numeric(investment < lag_investment), NA_real_),
    investor_stay = if_else(role == "investor" & !is.na(lag_investment), as.numeric(investment == lag_investment), NA_real_),
    trustee_delta_investment = if_else(role == "trustee" & !is.na(lag_investment), investment - lag_investment, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(game_id) %>%
  mutate(
    next_investment = lead(investment, default = 0),
    BPD_ctrst = factor(if_else(group == "BPD", 1, 0)),
    AD_ctrst = factor(if_else(group == "AD", 1, 0))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

safe_divide <- function(num, denom) {
  ifelse(denom > 0, num / denom, NA_real_)
}

z_score <- function(x) {
  # Manual z-score that gracefully handles zero-variance segments
  mu <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_x <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(sd_x) || sd_x == 0) {
    return(x * 0)
  }
  (x - mu) / sd_x
}

logit_transform <- function(p, eps = 1e-4) {
  # WARNING: Only use for values strictly in (0,1)
  # For return ratios that can exceed 1, use alternative approach
  p_adj <- pmin(pmax(p, eps), 1 - eps)
  log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
}

inv_logit <- function(x) {
  1 / (1 + exp(-x))
}

# Alternative transformation for return ratios that can be >1
# Uses a scaled logit that handles the full range
scaled_logit_transform <- function(x, eps = 1e-4, max_ratio = 3) {
  # Scale to (0, 1) range first, then apply logit
  x_scaled <- x / (max_ratio + eps)
  x_scaled <- pmin(pmax(x_scaled, eps), 1 - eps)
  log(x_scaled / (1 - x_scaled))
}

inv_scaled_logit <- function(y, max_ratio = 3) {
  # Inverse of scaled_logit_transform
  x_scaled <- 1 / (1 + exp(-y))
  x_scaled * max_ratio
}

investor_summary <- clean_dat %>%
  filter(role == "investor") %>%
  group_by(subject_ID) %>%
  summarise(
    invest_mean_first5 = mean(investment[round <= 5], na.rm = TRUE),
    invest_mean_last5 = mean(investment[round >= 6], na.rm = TRUE),
    invest_prop_first5 = mean((investment / 20)[round <= 5], na.rm = TRUE),
    invest_prop_last5 = mean((investment / 20)[round >= 6], na.rm = TRUE),
    investor_responsiveness_events = sum(investor_responsiveness_event, na.rm = TRUE),
    investor_responsiveness_opportunities = sum(!is.na(investor_responsiveness_event)),
    investor_responsiveness_rate = safe_divide(
      investor_responsiveness_events,
      investor_responsiveness_opportunities
    ),
    investor_retaliation_events = sum(investor_retaliation_event, na.rm = TRUE),
    investor_retaliation_opportunities = sum(!is.na(investor_retaliation_event)),
    investor_retaliation_rate = safe_divide(
      investor_retaliation_events,
      investor_retaliation_opportunities
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(role = "investor") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(is.nan(.x), NA_real_, .x)))

trustee_summary <- clean_dat %>%

    trust_coaxing_events = sum(trustee_coaxing_event, na.rm = TRUE),

    trust_encouragement_events = sum(trustee_encouragement_event, na.rm = TRUE),
    trust_encouragement_opportunities = sum(!is.na(trustee_encouragement_event)),

    trust_coop_pickup_events = sum(trustee_coop_pickup_event, na.rm = TRUE),
    trust_coop_pickup_opportunities = sum(!is.na(trustee_coop_pickup_event)),
    trust_coop_pickup_rate = safe_divide(
      trust_coop_pickup_events,
      trust_coop_pickup_opportunities
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(role = "trustee") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(is.nan(.x), NA_real_, .x)))

  count(role, name = "n")

group_role_counts <- participant_counts %>%
  count(role, group, name = "n")

group_counts <- participant_counts %>%
  count(group, name = "n")

safe_group_role_n <- function(role_value, group_value) {
  val <- group_role_counts %>%
    dplyr::filter(role == role_value, group == group_value) %>%
    dplyr::pull(n)
  if (length(val) == 0) 0 else val
}

safe_group_n <- function(group_value) {
  val <- group_counts %>%
    dplyr::filter(group == group_value) %>%
    dplyr::pull(n)
  if (length(val) == 0) 0 else val
}

n_total_participants <- nrow(participant_counts)
n_trustees <- role_counts$n[role_counts$role == "trustee"]
n_investors <- role_counts$n[role_counts$role == "investor"]
n_bpd_total <- safe_group_n("BPD")
n_ad_total <- safe_group_n("AD")
n_cc_total <- safe_group_n("CC")
n_mdd_trustees <- safe_group_role_n("trustee", "AD")
n_mdd_investors <- safe_group_role_n("investor", "AD")
```

# Abstract

Cooperation depends not only on how much people trust and reciprocate, but on how it is maintained and repaired after rupture. We analysed a 10-round Trust Game in participants with borderline personality disorder (BPD), an affective-symptom sample (AD), and community controls (N = `r scales::comma(n_total_participants)`; BPD *n* = `r scales::comma(n_bpd_total)`, AD *n* = `r scales::comma(n_ad_total)`, controls *n* = `r scales::comma(n_cc_total)`), using mixed-effects and hidden Markov models. Average behaviour was broadly similar across groups, although AD trustees returned more than controls. As investors, BPD participants adjusted less to feedback and made high investments less often than controls. Among trustees, AD differed most clearly from BPD: AD trustees followed cooperative response patterns more often, resumed cooperation more readily after exploitative returns, and had higher model-implied long-run cooperation. BPD–control differences in maintaining and restoring cooperation were smaller and depended on investment and on the hidden-state specification. Clinical differences were more evident in interaction dynamics than in average behaviour.

\newpage

# Introduction

Interpersonal dysfunction is a hallmark of many psychiatric conditions, yet characterising the dynamics through which cooperation unfolds and breaks down in these disorders remains methodologically challenging [@kupferberg2016social; @skodol2002personality]. Cooperation is not a unitary decision but a dynamic interpersonal process in which trust is extended, reciprocated, sometimes violated, and at times repaired [@fehr2003nature; @king-casas2008getting]. These dynamics plausibly depend, in part, on mentalizing, broadly understood as interpreting a partner's behaviour in terms of underlying intentions and using this information to guide one's own responses [@fonagy2004affect; @frith2012mentalizing]. Disruptions in mentalizing have been proposed as one pathway through which social learning and relationships deteriorate, particularly in borderline pathology [@fonagy2009developmental]. Identifying where and how cooperation fails in clinical populations therefore requires methods capable of capturing these dynamics rather than merely their endpoints.

The multi-round Trust Game (MRT) offers such a framework [@berg1995trust]. In each round, an investor decides how much of an endowment to send to a trustee; the transferred amount is multiplied, and the trustee then decides how much to return. Investor transfers index interpersonal trust, whereas trustee returns index reciprocity [@king-casas2005getting]. The repeated structure allows cooperation to emerge through generous exchanges, to be disrupted by defections, and potentially to be repaired through strategic signals such as *coaxing*, that is, fair returns following low investment in order to encourage the partner back into cooperation [@king-casas2008getting]. The MRT therefore captures not only how much individuals cooperate, but also how cooperation evolves over the course of an interaction [@baumgartner2008trust].

However, Trust Game studies that reduce behaviour to average investment or average return across rounds collapse these dynamics into a single summary index, and clinical studies have often relied on small samples (n < 50). Such approaches obscure the processes of greatest theoretical and clinical interest. Two individuals may show identical mean reciprocity while relying on markedly different strategies: one may sustain stable cooperation throughout, whereas another may alternate between generous and exploitative responses. If clinical groups differ not in *how much* they cooperate, but in *how* they cooperate — whether they maintain cooperation, how they respond to rupture, and whether they repair it — then aggregate averages are unlikely to detect these distinctions. Computational psychiatry seeks to move beyond such summary measures by fitting generative models that formalise the latent processes shaping observable behaviour [@montague2012computational; @huys2015computational].

Hidden Markov models (HMMs) provide a natural framework for this aim [@visser2022mixture]. HMMs represent behaviour as transitions between latent states whose number and characteristics are inferred from the data, with transition probabilities that may depend on task variables such as partner investment. In the MRT, the recovered states can be interpreted post hoc, for example, as exploitative, cautious, or cooperative modes of responding, on the basis of their emission distributions [@guennouni2025rebuilding]. Applied to cooperation data, the transition structure of an HMM can be interpreted in terms of clinically meaningful processes: *maintenance*, defined as the tendency to remain in cooperative states once entered, and *repair*, defined as the tendency to re-enter cooperation following a lapse. These capture distinct aspects of cooperation dynamics that are also psychologically distinguishable. Maintenance depends on the capacity to sustain a collaborative stance toward the partner in the face of weakly negative or ambiguous cues; repair depends on the capacity to recover that stance after a breakdown, treating a signal of renewed cooperative intent as genuine rather than as manipulation or irrelevance [@bateman2004mentalization]. Because these capacities are likely to draw on different psychological resources, they may be differentially disrupted across clinical groups, making the distinction between maintenance and repair especially important for empirical analysis.

Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterised by unstable relationships, affective lability, and rapid oscillation between idealisation and devaluation of others [@skodol2002personality; @gunderson2011borderline; @zanarini2007zanarini]. Several features of BPD may plausibly shape the dynamics of cooperation, and in a mentalizing and epistemic trust framework these features are deeply interconnected rather than independent. Mentalizing difficulties, central to developmental accounts of BPD [@fonagy2009developmental; @fonagy2004affect; @bateman2004mentalization], may impair flexible interpretation of a partner's intentions, particularly when signals are ambiguous. Under conditions of epistemic hypervigilance [@fonagy2017epistemic; @fonagy2015epistemic; @nolte2023epistemic], ambiguous cues such as low investment may be read not merely as low generosity but as socially meaningful signs of misattunement, disinterest, or impending abandonment. On this account, the core difficulty is not simply excessive affective reactivity, though emotion dysregulation [@linehan1993cognitive] may accelerate the process, but the collapse of a flexible interpretive stance toward the partner — a state in which the other person becomes harder to represent as having a mind that is both separate and benignly intelligible. Heightened rejection sensitivity [@staebler2011facial; @gunderson2011borderline] may compound this by amplifying negative readings of ambiguous signals and precipitating transitions out of cooperative states. Consistent with this account, Trust Game studies have reported reduced trust and reciprocity in BPD [@unoka2009trust; @king-casas2008getting]. @king-casas2008getting found that individuals with BPD could *initiate* cooperation but struggled to *sustain* it, showing reduced coaxing behaviour. Whether this difficulty reflects a failure to signal repair after rupture, as the coaxing account implies, or a more specific fragility in sustaining cooperation when partner signals are weak or ambiguous, remains an open question. In HMM terms, the former would predict impaired re-entry into cooperative states, whereas the latter would predict impaired retention within them.

Affective disorders (AD), used here as a shorthand label for the treatment-seeking subgroup with depressive and/or anxiety presentations in this study, present a more heterogeneous picture. Depression is associated with low mood, anhedonia, and impaired social functioning [@gotlib2010cognition; @kupferberg2016social], yet recent Trust Game evidence suggests intact or even *heightened* cooperative behaviour in depressed individuals [@ong2017increased], possibly reflecting interpersonal over-accommodation — a tendency to preserve the interaction by absorbing the burden of repair, consistent with guilt, submissiveness, and conflict avoidance [@oconnor2002guilt] — rather than finely calibrated responsiveness to partner signals. By contrast, social anxiety has been linked to *reduced* reciprocity, potentially reflecting interpersonal inhibition and difficulty responding to prosocial overtures [@anderl2018reduced]. These opposing tendencies raise the possibility that average reciprocity in a heterogeneous AD sample may conceal divergent underlying dynamics. A process-level analysis capable of distinguishing how cooperation is maintained and repaired is therefore needed to determine which aspects of cooperation are affected.

Guided by this framework, we analysed a large sample of community controls (CC), patients with BPD, and the affective-symptom subgroup (AD) who completed a 10-round MRT in either the investor or trustee role (N = `r scales::comma(n_total_participants)`; `r scales::comma(n_trustees)` trustees, `r scales::comma(n_investors)` investors). We combined trial-level mixed-effects models, which test how trust and reciprocity respond to partner behaviour from round to round, with HMMs, which characterise how cooperation is maintained and repaired through transitions between latent states. By examining both roles, we also asked whether clinical groups show role-dependent patterns in social exchange tasks [@nolte2025role]. Because the investor and trustee roles were completed by different participants, however, these comparisons are limited to the group level and do not permit within-person cross-role inference.

We hypothesised that BPD would show reduced reciprocity together with a distinct dynamic signature of fragile cooperation, including lower retention in cooperative states and weaker cooperative repair following rupture, consistent with the fragile cooperation pattern reported by @king-casas2008getting. For AD, prior findings suggest competing possibilities: depression has been associated with increased cooperation [@ong2017increased], whereas anxiety has been linked to reduced reciprocity [@anderl2018reduced]. We therefore adopted an exploratory approach to determine which pattern predominated in this sample. By contrasting maintenance and repair profiles across diagnostic groups, we aimed to identify distinct reciprocity phenotypes that may help refine mechanistic accounts of interpersonal dysfunction and inform more targeted clinical intervention.

# Transparency and Openness

## Preregistration

This study involved analysis of existing data rather than new data collection for this manuscript and was not preregistered. The analyses should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

## Data, Materials, Code, and Online Resources

Analysis code and manuscript sources are available in the [versioned code release](https://github.com/ismailg/trust-game-reciprocity-code/releases/tag/submission-v3). De-identified behavioural data may be shared with researchers upon reasonable request to the corresponding author, subject to approval by the relevant data custodians and applicable ethics and information-governance requirements. Identifiable participant data cannot be shared. Supplemental Material is provided in the separate file supplement.pdf.

## Reporting

This study involved analysis of existing data rather than new data collection for this manuscript. We report how the analytic sample was determined, all data exclusions, all task manipulations, and all measures used in the study.

## Ethical Approval and Compensation

The BPD/ASPD parent study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee for Wales (12/WA/0283), and the AD remote study was approved by the London Queen Square Research Ethics Committee (16/LO/0077). All participants provided written informed consent, and the approved protocols were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participants received £10 per hour, with optional performance-based incentives.

# Methods

## Participants

### Recruitment and Diagnostic Procedures

**BPD.** Adult patients meeting DSM-IV criteria for BPD were drawn from a larger study of social exchange in BPD and ASPD, “Probing Social Exchanges – A Computational Neuroscience Approach to the Understanding of Borderline and Antisocial Personality Disorder”. Patients with a pre-existing clinical diagnosis of BPD or ASPD were referred by psychiatrists, care coordinators, and trainee clinical psychologists working in personality disorder services across seven London NHS Mental Health Trusts spanning five London boroughs. Referrals were also received via a London Probation Trust-associated personality disorder screening system. Participants were assessed by experienced, trained clinical psychologists using the SCID-II [@first1997structured]. To support rating reliability, consensus conferences were held regularly under senior researcher supervision. The SCID-II has demonstrated adequate inter-rater reliability and internal consistency for the diagnosis of BPD in several studies, including @lobbestael2011inter and @maffei1997interrater. Inclusion criteria were a diagnosis of BPD and fluency in English. Exclusion criteria were recent psychotic episodes, severe learning disability, and current or past neurological disorder or trauma. From 2020 onwards, participants completed a remote version of the study protocol. Participants with ASPD were recruited in the parent study but excluded from the present analyses because of the small sample size (n = 10 trustees).

**AD.** No research-administered structured diagnostic interview was conducted in this subsample; accordingly, the AD group should be understood as a treatment-seeking affective-symptom sample throughout this paper, and all AD-related findings are treated as exploratory. AD participants were recruited through NHS IAPT services, now NHS Talking Therapies. Their depressive or anxiety presentations were established within the treating services by trained clinical staff using routine clinical assessment and service diagnostic descriptors. Participants were eligible if they (a) had clinically significant depressive or anxiety symptoms and (b) were assessed as suitable for low- or high-intensity face-to-face therapy within IAPT; those scoring above the SCID-II screening-questionnaire cut-off were excluded. These participants completed a remote version of the study, which included the same self-report measures and one behavioural task. Additional exclusion criteria were recent psychotic episodes, severe learning disability, and current or past neurological disorder or trauma. We retain the shorthand label AD for brevity; however, inferences relating to this group should be interpreted as applying to treatment-seeking affective-symptom service users rather than to depression or anxiety populations more generally.

**CC.** Healthy participants were recruited from community settings, including the internet, notice boards, universities, and job centres, and were screened using the SAPAS [@moran2003sapas]. In the original validation study, a cut-off score of 3 showed 94% sensitivity and 85% specificity for DSM-IV personality disorder in psychiatric patients [@moran2003sapas]. Individuals scoring 3 or above on the SAPAS were excluded from the control group.

### Inclusion criteria and attrition

After collating all raw files, extracting MRT data, and cross-referencing participants with diagnostic categories, we identified `r scales::comma(total_attrition$n_initial_total)` participants who had completed the 10-round MRT. To ensure data quality and compatibility with the trial-level modelling approach, we excluded participants with incomplete task data. Specifically, participants were removed if they did not have at least one observation recorded for each of the 10 rounds, including cases with missing or duplicate round entries. This criterion resulted in the exclusion of `r total_attrition$n_excluded_total` participants.

The final analytic sample comprised `r scales::comma(n_total_participants)` unique participants, including `r scales::comma(n_trustees)` trustees and `r scales::comma(n_investors)` investors. Diagnostic groups were recruited independently and were not individually matched on demographic variables. Exclusions were rare (`r total_attrition$percent_excluded`%; `r attrition_group_test_name`, *p* `r attrition_group_p`) and did not differ detectably across diagnostic groups (Table \@ref(tab:sample-attrition)). AD investors ($n = `r n_mdd_investors`$) were underrepresented relative to the other cells; contrasts involving this group should therefore be interpreted cautiously. The present analyses were conducted on a fixed sample accumulated across the parent studies rather than on a sample prospectively powered for the current hypotheses. Demographic characteristics, including age and gender, are reported in Table \@ref(tab:sample-attrition). Primary analyses focused on diagnostic-group effects. Sensitivity analyses adjusting for available demographic covariates and for administration mode (BEH/MRI/WEB) are reported as robustness checks in Supplement Tables S11, S12, S15, and S16, rather than being incorporated into the primary model set.

# Add totals row

# Demographics summary for final analytic sample
demo_lookup <- read.csv("Data/demographics.csv",

demo_lookup <- demo_lookup %>%

demo_stats <- demo_summary %>%

attrition_display <- attrition_display %>%

## MRT Paradigm

Participants completed a 10-round MRT [@berg1995trust]. In each round, investors received 20 tokens and decided how many to send to a trustee. The transferred amount was tripled, after which the trustee decided how much to return. Participants remained in the same role throughout the task.

Participants were told that they were paired with another player. In fact, the partner was a computerised agent implementing a nearest-neighbour response algorithm. On each trial, the agent constructed a state representation from the current investment and interaction history, including the previous investment and previous return, searched a library of prior human responses for the closest matching state, and replayed the corresponding response. The agent could produce locally exploitative or generous responses from the library, but did not learn participant-specific policies across rounds. This version of the MRT therefore assessed responses to controlled social signals under presumed human agency, rather than genuinely reciprocal interpersonal dynamics in which both partners adapt to each other.

## Behavioural feature definitions

In addition to mean investment and return levels, we defined trial-level behavioural events to capture dynamic reciprocity patterns. For descriptive summaries, these events were aggregated to participant-level rates; in the mixed-effects analyses, they entered as binary outcomes. A fair return equalises investor and trustee payoffs and was defined as $\text{fair return} = 2 \times \text{investment} - 10$ when investment $\geq 5$ tokens, and 0 otherwise. For example, if investment = 10 tokens, the trustee receives 30; a fair return of 10 tokens would leave both parties with 20 tokens each. For investments < 5 tokens, equal payoffs are mathematically impossible under the tripling rule. In these low-investment cases, we therefore defined the fair-return floor as 0, meaning that any positive return was classified as "better than fair". Full feature formulae and coding details are provided in Supplement S1.1.

For investors, we examined two forms of adjustment to trustee behaviour. Responsiveness was defined as the tendency to increase investment following better-than-fair returns, indexing positive reciprocity. Retaliation was defined as the tendency to decrease investment following worse-than-fair returns, indexing negative reciprocity.

For trustees, we examined three forms of response to investor stakes. Coaxing was defined as returning at least the invested amount after low but non-zero investments ($0 < \text{investment} \leq 5$ tokens). Encouragement was coded when the investor sent fewer tokens than in the preceding round but the trustee returned more tokens than in that round—for example, when investment fell from 10 to 5 tokens while the return rose from 8 to 9 tokens. Cooperation pick-up was coded when both the investment and the number of tokens returned increased from the preceding round—for example, from 5 tokens invested and 4 returned to 10 invested and 6 returned.


## Statistical analyses

### Linear mixed-effects models

We used LMMs to analyse trial-level behaviour while accounting for within-participant dependence across the 10 rounds [@matuschek2017balancing]. Models were estimated in R using the lme4 and lmerTest packages. Unless otherwise stated, *p*-values were based on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; spot checks using Kenward–Roger corrections yielded the same inferential pattern. We report fixed-effect estimates, 95% CIs, and tests of marginal means. Our primary diagnostic questions concerned whether each clinical group differed from CC. We therefore estimated two focal treatment-versus-control contrasts, BPD vs CC and AD vs CC, using the emmeans package [@emmeans]. For transparency, the corresponding estimates are reported in the main text, but inferential claims are based on Holm-adjusted *p*-values within each model family. Exploratory pairwise comparisons beyond these focal contrasts are retained in the Supplement and were likewise Holm-adjusted within family.

We report unstandardised coefficients with 95% CIs, which are directly interpretable in the original metric, tokens for investment and logit units for the proportion of the tripled amount returned, supplemented where informative by simple-slope comparisons and percentage-change metrics (see Supplement S1.2 for the rationale).

#### Investor investment model

We compared four nested investor models: (a) diagnosis only, (b) diagnosis plus round and lagged net return main effects, (c) all two-way interactions, and (d) the three-way interaction. The best-fitting model was selected using sequential likelihood-ratio tests across the nested hierarchy. Random effects included participant-specific intercepts and slopes for lagged net return.

```{r investorLMM, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
# Investor LMM code appears in the Results section below
# Setting this chunk to not display for Methods section
```

#### Trustee return model

We compared four nested trustee models: (a) group only, (b) group plus round and investment main effects, (c) all two-way interactions, and (d) the three-way interaction. The best-fitting model was selected using sequential likelihood-ratio tests across the nested hierarchy. We initially attempted random-slope specifications for investment, but the two-way and three-way interaction models failed to converge under that random-effects structure. LMM convergence checks used retry-based optimizer fitting, with `bobyqa` as the primary optimizer and `nloptwrap` as a fallback when needed; uncorrelated intercept-and-slope variants were not additionally evaluated. To preserve valid likelihood-ratio comparisons on a common estimable random-effects structure, all trustee models in the hierarchy were therefore fitted with random intercepts only. Random-intercept-only models may underestimate standard errors for investment-related fixed effects, and the trustee LMM results should be interpreted with this caveat in mind.

### Trial-level behavioural event models

To model the trial-level behavioural events without discarding contextual information, we fitted hierarchical logistic GLMMs to each binary outcome: investor responsiveness, investor retaliation, trustee coaxing, trustee encouragement, and trustee cooperation pick-up. This approach accommodates varying denominators and allows partial pooling across sparse diagnostic groups.

For investor responsiveness and retaliation, the binary outcomes defined above were modelled as a function of the previous round's fairness gap, z-scored, prior investment, z-scored, round, modelled with a natural spline (2 df), and diagnosis.

For trustee coaxing, encouragement, and cooperation pick-up, the binary outcomes defined above were modelled as a function of current and prior investments, both z-scored, the previous round's fairness gap, z-scored, round, modelled with a natural spline (2 df), and diagnostic group.

For diagnosis effects in the GLMMs, we used the same two focal treatment-versus-control contrasts against CC estimated with emmeans. Estimates are reported in the main text, but inferential claims are based on Holm-adjusted *p*-values within model family. When random-slope specifications were singular or produced convergence warnings in sparse behavioural subsets, the models were simplified to random intercepts only, and the retained random-effects structure is reported.

## Hidden Markov models

Because reciprocity unfolds over time and may reflect unobserved shifts in strategy, we used HMMs to identify latent states directly from behavioural sequences rather than imposing fixed categories. HMMs represent observed behaviour as emissions from a sequence of discrete latent states linked by probabilistic transitions, allowing both the number and the characteristics of these states to be estimated from the data. Models were fitted in R using the `depmixS4` package [@visser2010depmixs4], and interpretive labels were assigned only after estimation on the basis of the recovered emission profiles. Prior simulation work in an independent repeated Trust Game dataset demonstrated recovery of the ordered state policies and state-occupancy quantities used to interpret this model class [@guennouni2025rebuilding].

### Model specification and fitting

We fitted separate HMM families for investors and trustees, considering models with 2 to 7 latent states in each role. Trustee models included CC, BPD, and AD participants. Because the AD investor cell was small ($n = `r n_mdd_investors`$), investor HMMs were fitted to CC and BPD sequences only. Within each role, models were estimated on pooled participant sequences. Trustee returns were modelled within their feasible range conditional on current investment, and investor emissions were bounded to the observed 0 to 20 token investment scale. Transitions depended on partner investment on the following round for trustees and prior-round net return for investors. At each state count, we fitted one model in which transitions depended on the role-specific trial variable and another that also included diagnostic group and its interaction with that variable. Each candidate was fitted from multiple starting values, retaining the converged solution with the highest likelihood. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selected the number of states within the models that included diagnostic group. At the selected state count, we used a likelihood-ratio test to assess whether the group terms improved model fit and retained them when they did [@giudici2000likelihood]. Full fitting details are provided in Supplement S1.3–S1.4.

### Estimating and analysing latent states

An HMM does not determine a trial’s latent state with certainty. After fitting, the forward–backward algorithm used the complete 10-round sequence to estimate the probability that each trial belonged to each state [@visser2010depmixs4]. We retained these probabilities when estimating transitions and their uncertainty, allowing each pair of consecutive trials to contribute partly to several possible transitions. For other analyses, we assigned each trial to the state with the highest probability, considering each trial separately. We refer to analyses based on this sequence as most-likely-state analyses. To summarise how confidently trials could be assigned, we report the mean probability of each trial’s most likely state and the proportion of trials assigned with a probability of at least .80.

In both roles, the most-likely-state sequences were used to calculate each participant’s occupancy of each state, defined as the proportion of trials assigned to that state. We compared these proportions across groups using one-way ANOVAs and applied Holm correction to each set of occupancy comparisons. The comparisons included in each correction are reported in the Supplement.

We then examined how participants moved between states from one round to the next. For investors, each state was represented by its mean investment. Net earnings were defined as the amount returned minus the amount invested. We tested whether net earnings predicted the investment level of the next state and whether this relationship differed between BPD and CC. The model also accounted for the current state. For trustees, separate models examined remaining cooperative, returning to cooperation from the exploitative or neutral state, and leaving cooperation for either state. We tested whether these outcomes varied with the partner’s next investment and diagnosis.

### Transition dynamics and reciprocity metrics

State occupancy describes which strategies are expressed, but reciprocity also depends on how strategies change over time. The cooperation-focused transition analyses therefore centred on the trustee HMMs, in which states with higher return emissions can be interpreted as more cooperative and states with lower return emissions as more exploitative. After ordering trustee states by their emission means, we treated the fitted transition model as a covariate-dependent Markov chain and evaluated it at representative investment levels of 5, 10, and 15 tokens. In the selected five-state model, State 1 returned well below one third of the tripled investment and was classified as exploitative. State 2 was centred near one third, which returned approximately the investor’s original stake, and was classified as neutral. States 3–5 returned more than one third and were classified as cooperative. These labels describe the economic consequences of the fitted return distributions. From these transition matrices, we derived four metrics: *retention*, the probability of remaining in cooperative states; *repair*, the probability of moving from exploitative State 1 into cooperative States 3–5; *exploitative exit*, the probability of leaving cooperative states for State 1; and *model-implied long-run cooperation*, the eventual probability of occupying cooperative states if the partner repeated the same investment level across rounds. This final quantity was calculated from the invariant distribution of the corresponding transition matrix. Movement from neutral State 2 into cooperation and movement from cooperation into State 2 were examined separately.

Because all four metrics are derived from the same transition matrix, they describe related aspects of the same transition pattern and were interpreted together. When retention or exploitative exit combined several cooperative starting states, we averaged the state-specific transition probabilities according to how frequently those states occurred in the model’s long-run distribution. Unlike the mixed-model analyses, which focused on two focal clinical-versus-control contrasts, the HMM transition analyses were used to characterise relative reciprocity phenotypes across all diagnostic groups. We therefore retained all pairwise diagnostic comparisons in the HMM summaries, including AD vs BPD, and applied Holm correction within each HMM comparison family. The comparisons included in each family are reported in Supplement S1.3.

```

We quantified uncertainty in the trustee transition measures using a transition-only bootstrap. We obtained 10,000 successfully fitted bootstrap samples for the five-state model. Point estimates were taken directly from the fitted HMM. CIs were calculated as percentile intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles), and hypothesis tests were based on two-sided bootstrap *p*-values with Holm correction within the comparison families described above.

The bootstrap varied the transition counts and transition parameters while keeping the five-state structure and its state-specific return distributions fixed. The resulting intervals and *p*-values therefore describe uncertainty in the transition dynamics of the selected five-state model. We repeated the analyses with neighbouring four- and six-state models, using 10,000 successful bootstrap samples per model. Further details are reported in Supplement S1.3.

The primary trustee hidden-state analysis included all `r n_trustees` trustees. For model-implied long-run cooperation, sensitivity analyses included online trustees (*n* = `r trustee_long_run_sens_n[["online_only"]]`) and the online participants with complete demographic data (*n* = `r trustee_long_run_sens_n[["online_complete_case"]]`), analysed before and after age and gender adjustment. Each analysis used `r scales::comma(trustee_long_run_sens_boot_n)` successful transition-bootstrap samples. An additional demographic-adjusted analysis across all testing settings is reported in the supplement.

## Investor behaviour analysis

```{r investor-lmm-data, include=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
## ---- Investor LMM data and helpers --------------------------------------
## This chunk (i) prepares the investor dataset, (ii) defines the optimizer
## controls, and (iii) sets up general-purpose helper functions that every
## subsequent chunk reuses for convergence checking/logging.
## 1. Assemble the investor-level dataset with centered predictors
inv_dat <- clean_dat %>%
  filter(role == "investor") %>%
  arrange(subject_ID, round) %>%
  group_by(subject_ID) %>%
  mutate(lag_net_return = lag(return - investment)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  drop_na(lag_net_return) %>%
  mutate(
    group = factor(group, levels = c("CC", "BPD", "AD")),
    round_c = scale(round, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)[, 1],
    lag_net_return_c = scale(lag_net_return, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)[, 1]
  )

## 2. Use treatment contrasts for fixed effects so emmeans behaves predictably
old_contrasts <- getOption("contrasts")
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

## 3. Shared optimizer settings, retries, and convergence helpers
strict_lmer_ctrl <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = "bobyqa",
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e6),
  calc.derivs = TRUE
)
fallback_lmer_ctrl <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = "nloptwrap",
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e6),
  calc.derivs = TRUE
)
gradient_tol <- 0.002
fit_controls <- list(
  list(name = "bobyqa", ctrl = strict_lmer_ctrl),
  list(name = "nloptwrap", ctrl = fallback_lmer_ctrl)
)

quiet_status <- function() isTRUE(getOption("vtc.quiet_convergence"))
emit_status <- function(...) {
  if (!quiet_status()) {
    cat(..., sep = "")
  }
}
get_max_grad <- function(fit) {
  grad <- tryCatch(fit@optinfo$derivs$grad, error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(grad)) return(NA_real_)
  max(abs(grad))
}
## fit_with_retry() attempts each optimizer in sequence, logging diagnostics and
## returning the first converged fit (or NULL if none converge).
## Convergence is determined by optimizer success (code 0) and absence of lme4 warnings.
## High gradients are logged as warnings but do not reject the fit.
fit_with_retry <- function(formula, data, label, REML_flag = FALSE) {
  for (cfg in fit_controls) {
    attempt <- tryCatch(
      lmer(formula, data = data, REML = REML_flag, control = cfg$ctrl),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (is.null(attempt)) {
      emit_status(sprintf("[%s | %s] fit failed (skipping).\n", label, cfg$name))
      next
    }
    grad <- get_max_grad(attempt)
    conv_msg <- attempt@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages
    opt_code <- attempt@optinfo$conv$opt
    # Accept if optimizer converged (code 0) and no lme4 warnings
    converged <- (opt_code == 0) && is.null(conv_msg)
    # Log gradient warning if above threshold (soft check)
    grad_warning <- !is.na(grad) && grad > gradient_tol
    emit_status(sprintf(
      "[%s | %s] max|grad| = %s%s, converged = %s\n",
      label, cfg$name,
      ifelse(is.na(grad), "NA", scales::number(grad, accuracy = 0.0001)),
      ifelse(grad_warning, " (above threshold)", ""),
      converged
    ))
    if (converged) {
      return(list(
        fit = attempt,
        max_grad = grad,
        control_name = cfg$name
      ))
    }
  }
  emit_status(sprintf("[%s] Dropped from comparison (no converged optimizer).\n", label))
  return(NULL)
}

```



```{r investor-lmm-ml, include=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
## ---- Investor LMM ML fits -----------------------------------------------
## This chunk runs the ML portion of the nested-model workflow: fit each
## candidate, drop non-converged stages, and compute the LR tables.
## 4. Define model hierarchy and fit each stage with retries
inv_model_specs <- list(
  list(
    label = "Baseline (Group only)",
    stage = "m0",
    formula = investment ~ group + (1 | subject_ID)
  ),
  list(
    label = "Main Effects",
    stage = "m1",
    formula = investment ~ group + round_c + lag_net_return_c +
      (1 + lag_net_return_c | subject_ID)
  ),
  list(
    label = "Two-Way Interaction",
    stage = "m2",
    formula = investment ~ group * round_c + group * lag_net_return_c +
      (1 + lag_net_return_c | subject_ID)
  ),
  list(
    label = "Three-Way Interaction",
    stage = "m3",
    formula = investment ~ group * round_c * lag_net_return_c +
      (1 + lag_net_return_c | subject_ID)
  )
)

inv_ml_fits <- purrr::map(inv_model_specs, function(spec) {
  fit_obj <- fit_with_retry(
    formula = spec$formula,
    data = inv_dat,
    label = spec$label,
    REML_flag = FALSE
  )
  if (is.null(fit_obj)) return(NULL)
  c(fit_obj, list(stage = spec$stage, label = spec$label, formula = spec$formula))
}) %>%
  purrr::compact()

if (length(inv_ml_fits) < 2) {
  stop("Fewer than two investor ML models converged; unable to run likelihood-ratio comparisons.")
}

stage_order <- purrr::map_chr(inv_ml_fits, "stage")
purrr::walk(inv_ml_fits, function(entry) {
  emit_status(sprintf(
    "[Investor ML] %s retained (optimizer: %s, max|grad| = %s)\n",
    entry$label,
    entry$control_name,
    ifelse(is.null(entry$max_grad), "NA", scales::number(entry$max_grad, accuracy = 0.0001))
  ))
})
inv_model_list <- inv_ml_fits %>%
  purrr::set_names(purrr::map_chr(., "label")) %>%
  purrr::map("fit")

## 5. Tabulate AICs and run sequential likelihood-ratio tests on converged models
aic_tbl <- tibble(
  Model = names(inv_model_list),
  AIC = purrr::map_dbl(inv_model_list, AIC)
)

if (length(inv_model_list) >= 2) {
  lr_raw <- do.call(anova, unname(inv_model_list))
  lr_raw_comp <- if (nrow(lr_raw) > 1) lr_raw[-1, , drop = FALSE] else lr_raw[FALSE, , drop = FALSE]
  stage_compare <- stage_order[-1]
  lr_tbl <- broom::tidy(lr_raw)
  lr_stage_tbl <- tibble(
    stage = stage_compare,
    Chisq = lr_raw_comp$Chisq,
    Df = lr_raw_comp$Df,
    p = lr_raw_comp$`Pr(>Chisq)`
  )
  lr_two_way_info <- lr_stage_tbl %>% filter(stage == "m2")
  lr_three_way_info <- lr_stage_tbl %>% filter(stage == "m3")
  lr_two_way_chisq <- if (nrow(lr_two_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_two_way_info$Chisq
  lr_two_way_df <- if (nrow(lr_two_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_two_way_info$Df
  lr_two_way_p <- if (nrow(lr_two_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_two_way_info$p
  lr_three_way_chisq <- if (nrow(lr_three_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_three_way_info$Chisq
  lr_three_way_df <- if (nrow(lr_three_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_three_way_info$Df
  lr_three_way_p <- if (nrow(lr_three_way_info) == 0) NA_real_ else lr_three_way_info$p
} else {
  emit_status("[Investor ML] Only one model converged; LR tests skipped.\n")
  lr_raw <- data.frame(`Pr(>Chisq)` = NA_real_)
  lr_tbl <- tibble()
  lr_stage_tbl <- tibble()
  lr_two_way_info <- lr_three_way_info <- tibble()
  lr_two_way_chisq <- lr_two_way_df <- lr_two_way_p <- lr_three_way_p <- NA_real_
}

```

```{r investor-lmm-reml, include=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
## ---- Investor LMM REML + diagnostics ------------------------------------
## Final chunk: choose LR-selected model, refit with REML (with retries),
## print the final gradient, and collect residual diagnostics for reporting.
## 6. Choose the simplest model that still improves fit
inv_lr_pvals <- lr_raw$`Pr(>Chisq)`
best_index <- 1
comparison_indices <- seq_along(inv_lr_pvals)
if (length(comparison_indices) > 1) {
  for (i in comparison_indices[-1]) {
    pval <- inv_lr_pvals[i]
    if (is.na(pval) || pval >= 0.05) break
    best_index <- i
  }
}

best_model_label <- names(inv_model_list)[best_index]
best_model_entry <- inv_ml_fits[[best_index]]

inv_lr_description <- if (!is.na(lr_two_way_chisq)) {
  glue::glue(
    "Sequential likelihood ratio tests favored the two-way interaction model ($m_2$) over the main-effects model (*$\\chi^2$* = {scales::number(lr_two_way_chisq, accuracy = 0.01)}, df = {lr_two_way_df}, *p* = {format_pval(lr_two_way_p)}). Adding the three-way interaction offered no additional benefit (*p* = {format_pval(lr_three_way_p)})."
  )
} else {
  glue::glue(
    "Sequential likelihood ratio tests indicated that the *Three-Way Interaction* model provided a significantly better fit than the Main Effects model ($\\chi^2$({lr_three_way_df}) = {scales::number(lr_three_way_chisq, accuracy = 0.01)}, *p* = {format_pval(lr_three_way_p)}). We therefore retained this specification and refit it with REML to obtain the final parameter estimates."
  )
}

## 7. Refit the chosen model with REML (again checking convergence)
best_reml <- fit_with_retry(
  formula = best_model_entry$formula,
  data = inv_dat,
  label = paste0(best_model_label, " (REML)"),
  REML_flag = TRUE
)
if (is.null(best_reml)) {
  stop("Selected investor model failed to converge under REML.")
}
inv_lmm <- best_reml$fit
inv_max_grad <- best_reml$max_grad
inv_max_grad_fmt <- ifelse(
  is.na(inv_max_grad),
  "NA",
  scales::number(inv_max_grad, accuracy = 0.0001)
)

emit_status(sprintf(
  "\n[Investor LMM] Selected model: %s | max|grad| = %s\n",
  best_model_label, inv_max_grad_fmt
))

## 9. Residual diagnostics for the Methods narrative
inv_res <- residuals(inv_lmm)
inv_fit <- fitted(inv_lmm)
inv_z <- as.numeric(scale(inv_res))
inv_outlier_pct <- mean(abs(inv_z) > 3, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
set.seed(1)
inv_sw <- shapiro.test(sample(inv_res, min(5000, length(inv_res))))
inv_centered <- inv_res - mean(inv_res)
inv_sd <- sd(inv_res)
inv_skew <- ifelse(inv_sd > 0, mean(inv_centered^3) / (inv_sd^3), NA_real_)
inv_kurt <- ifelse(inv_sd > 0, mean(inv_centered^4) / (inv_sd^4) - 3, NA_real_)
inv_breaks <- unique(quantile(inv_fit, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11), na.rm = TRUE))
if (length(inv_breaks) < 2 || all(!is.finite(inv_breaks))) inv_breaks <- range(inv_fit, na.rm = TRUE)
inv_bins <- tryCatch(cut(inv_fit, breaks = inv_breaks, include_lowest = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
inv_var_by_bin <- if (is.null(inv_bins)) NA_real_ else tapply(inv_res, inv_bins, var, na.rm = TRUE)
inv_var_ratio <- if (all(is.na(inv_var_by_bin))) NA_real_ else {
  max(inv_var_by_bin, na.rm = TRUE) / max(min(inv_var_by_bin, na.rm = TRUE), .Machine$double.eps)
}

## ---- Generate Supplement Table S3: Complete Investor LMM Output --------
inv_lmm_summary <- summary(inv_lmm)
inv_coef_table <- as.data.frame(coef(inv_lmm_summary))
inv_coef_table$Parameter <- rownames(inv_coef_table)
inv_coef_table <- inv_coef_table[, c("Parameter", "Estimate", "Std. Error", "df", "t value", "Pr(>|t|)")]
colnames(inv_coef_table) <- c("Parameter", "Estimate", "SE", "df", "t", "p")

# Format for supplement
inv_coef_supp <- inv_coef_table %>%
  mutate(
    Estimate = sprintf("%.4f", Estimate),
    SE = sprintf("%.4f", SE),
    df = sprintf("%.1f", df),
    t = sprintf("%.2f", t),
    p = ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
  )

# Save to supplement folder
if (!dir.exists("supplement")) dir.create("supplement")
write.csv(inv_coef_supp, "supplement/TableS3_Investor_LMM_Complete.csv", row.names = FALSE)

emit_status("\n[Supplement S3] Saved complete Investor LMM output table\n")

options(contrasts = old_contrasts)
```

### Investment sensitivity to returns across trials

Sequential likelihood ratio tests selected the two-way interaction model over main effects ($\chi^2$(`r lr_two_way_df`) = `r scales::number(lr_two_way_chisq, accuracy = 0.01)`, *p* `r format_pval_clause(lr_two_way_p)`); the three-way interaction offered no improvement (*p* `r format_pval_clause(lr_three_way_p)`). Full investor LMM model comparison and coefficient tables are provided in Supplement Tables S2–S4.

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

apa_flex(aic_tbl,
         caption = "Investor LMM model comparison (smaller AIC is better)")

apa_flex(lr_tbl,
         caption = "Likelihood ratio tests comparing nested investor LMMs")

tab_inv <- broom.mixed::tidy(inv_lmm, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(term = dplyr::recode(term,
                              "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
                              "round_c" = "round (centered)",
                              "lag_net_return_c" = "lag_net_return (centered)",
                              "round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "round_c × lag_net_return_c",
                              "groupBPD" = "Diagnosis: BPD",
                              "groupAD" = "Diagnosis: AD",
                              "groupBPD:round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × round_c × lag_net_return_c",
                              "groupAD:round_c:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × round_c × lag_net_return_c",
                              "groupBPD:round_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × round",
                              "groupAD:round_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × round",
                              "groupBPD:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: BPD × lag_net_return",
                              "groupAD:lag_net_return_c" = "Diagnosis: AD × lag_net_return"),
         Term = paste0(term, add_stars(p.value))) %>%
  dplyr::select(Term,
                Estimate = estimate,
                `Std Error` = std.error,
                `95% CI Lower` = conf.low,
                `95% CI Upper` = conf.high,
                Statistic = statistic,
                `p-value` = p.value) %>%
  mutate(
    Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
    `Std Error` = round(`Std Error`, 3),
    `95% CI Lower` = round(`95% CI Lower`, 3),
    `95% CI Upper` = round(`95% CI Upper`, 3),

  )

```{r extract-lmm-values, echo=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
# Extract key coefficient values for inline reporting
investor_coef_table <- summary(inv_lmm)$coefficients

safe_coef_pull <- function(tbl, term, column) {
  if (!term %in% rownames(tbl)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  tbl[term, column, drop = TRUE]
}

lag_net_return_coef <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "lag_net_return_c", "Estimate")
lag_net_return_t <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "lag_net_return_c", "t value")
lag_net_return_p <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "lag_net_return_c", "Pr(>|t|)")

bpd_interaction_coef <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "groupBPD:lag_net_return_c", "Estimate")
bpd_interaction_t <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "groupBPD:lag_net_return_c", "t value")
bpd_interaction_p <- safe_coef_pull(investor_coef_table, "groupBPD:lag_net_return_c", "Pr(>|t|)")

# Extract simple slopes from lag_slopes_df
hc_slope <- lag_slopes_df %>%
  filter(group == "CC") %>%
  pull(lag_net_return_c.trend)
bpd_slope <- lag_slopes_df %>%
  filter(group == "BPD") %>%
  pull(lag_net_return_c.trend)

# Calculate percentage difference
pct_diff <- if (is.na(hc_slope) || is.na(bpd_slope) || hc_slope == 0) NA_real_ else round(100 * abs(bpd_slope - hc_slope) / hc_slope, 0)

# Extract random effects SD
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(inv_lmm))
re_intercept_sd <- vc$sdcor[is.na(vc$var2) & vc$var1 == "(Intercept)"]
re_intercept_sd <- if (length(re_intercept_sd) > 0) re_intercept_sd[1] else NA_real_
re_slope_sd <- vc$sdcor[is.na(vc$var2) & vc$var1 == "lag_net_return_c"]
re_slope_sd <- if (length(re_slope_sd) > 0) re_slope_sd[1] else NA_real_

fmt_stat <- function(x, digits = 0.01, fallback = "n/a") {
  ifelse(is.na(x), fallback, scales::number(x, accuracy = digits))
}
fmt_pval <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "n/a", format_pval(x))

lag_effect_beta <- fmt_stat(lag_net_return_coef, 0.01)
lag_effect_t <- fmt_stat(lag_net_return_t, 0.01)
lag_effect_p <- fmt_pval(lag_net_return_p)

bpd_effect_beta <- fmt_stat(bpd_interaction_coef, 0.001)
bpd_effect_t <- fmt_stat(bpd_interaction_t, 0.01)
bpd_effect_p <- fmt_pval(bpd_interaction_p)

hc_slope_fmt <- fmt_stat(hc_slope, 0.01)
bpd_slope_fmt <- fmt_stat(bpd_slope, 0.01)
pct_diff_fmt <- ifelse(is.na(pct_diff), "n/a", scales::number(pct_diff, accuracy = 1))
re_intercept_sd_fmt <- fmt_stat(re_intercept_sd, 0.01)
re_slope_sd_fmt <- fmt_stat(re_slope_sd, 0.01)
```

Strong adaptation to feedback emerged across all groups: investors adjusted stakes proportionally to prior outcomes (lagged net return: $\beta = `r lag_effect_beta`$, $t = `r lag_effect_t`$, *p* `r format_pval_clause(lag_net_return_p)`). A significant BPD × lagged-return interaction ($\beta = `r bpd_effect_beta`$, $t = `r bpd_effect_t`$, *p* `r format_pval_clause(bpd_interaction_p)`) revealed attenuated adaptation in BPD: CC investors shifted next-round offers by $`r hc_slope_fmt`$ tokens per unit of prior profit, whereas BPD investors adjusted by only $`r bpd_slope_fmt`$ tokens—`r pct_diff_fmt`% smaller (Figure \@ref(fig:investor-behaviour-panel)B). This interaction was preserved across the range of feedback values. No main effects of diagnostic group on baseline investment or round number emerged. Large random-intercept variance ($\sigma = `r re_intercept_sd_fmt`$) indicated substantial individual heterogeneity beyond diagnosis.

We next examined whether these slope differences were also evident in trial-level tactical choices, specifically responsiveness and retaliation.

```{r investor-learning-slopes, include=FALSE, eval=!rtg_state_ready}
# Create prediction grid for CC and BPD across range of lagged net return
lag_range <- seq(

  min(inv_dat$lag_net_return_c, na.rm = TRUE),

  max(inv_dat$lag_net_return_c, na.rm = TRUE),
  length.out = 100
)

# Get model predictions using emmeans for proper uncertainty
library(emmeans)

# Create reference grid for CC and BPD only
emm_grid <- emmeans(inv_lmm, ~ group * lag_net_return_c, 
                     at = list(lag_net_return_c = lag_range,
                               group = c("CC", "BPD")),
                     cov.reduce = FALSE)

# Convert to data frame for plotting with confidence limits (compute if absent)
pred_df <- as.data.frame(emm_grid) %>%
  rename(investment = emmean, lag_net_return_c = lag_net_return_c) %>%
  mutate(
    crit = ifelse(is.na(df), qnorm(0.975), qt(0.975, df)),
    lower.CL = investment - crit * SE,
    upper.CL = investment + crit * SE,
    # Convert centered lag back to original scale for interpretability
    lag_net_return = lag_net_return_c + mean(inv_dat$lag_net_return, na.rm = TRUE),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("CC", "BPD"))
  )

# Plot with confidence ribbons
investor_learning_plot <- ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = lag_net_return, y = investment, color = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors[c("CC", "BPD")], name = "Diagnosis") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors[c("CC", "BPD")], name = "Diagnosis") +
  labs(
    x = "Lagged net return (tokens)",
    y = "Predicted investment (tokens)"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50", alpha = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 19.2,
           label = "Break-even", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 2.8, color = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(t = 8)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(r = 8)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey30"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.3),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = c(0.04, 0.96),
    legend.justification = c(0, 1),
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = scales::alpha("white", 0.85), color = NA),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

```{r investor-trial-glmm, include=FALSE, results='hide', eval=!rtg_state_ready}
old_contrasts <- getOption("contrasts")
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

investor_trial_base <- clean_dat %>%
  filter(role == "investor", !is.na(lag_investment)) %>%
  mutate(
    prev_stake_sc   = scale(lag_investment)[, 1],
    lag_fair_gap_sc = scale(lag_fair_gap)[, 1],
    invest_increase = as.numeric(investment > lag_investment),
    invest_decrease = as.numeric(investment < lag_investment),
    eligible_resp   = (lag_better_than_fair == TRUE & headroom_up == 1),
    eligible_retal  = (lag_worse_than_fair == TRUE & headroom_down == 1)
  )

resp_df <- investor_trial_base %>% filter(eligible_resp, !is.na(invest_increase))
ret_df  <- investor_trial_base %>% filter(eligible_retal, !is.na(invest_decrease))

resp_mod <- glmer(
  invest_increase ~ lag_fair_gap_sc + prev_stake_sc + splines::ns(round, df = 2) + group + (1 + lag_fair_gap_sc | subject_ID),
  data = resp_df,
  family = binomial,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)

ret_mod <- glmer(
  invest_decrease ~ lag_fair_gap_sc + prev_stake_sc + splines::ns(round, df = 2) + group + (1 + lag_fair_gap_sc | subject_ID),
  data = ret_df,
  family = binomial,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)

mk_inv_glmm <- function(mod, label) {
  res <- broom.mixed::tidy(mod, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
  if (!"p.value" %in% names(res)) {
    res <- res %>% mutate(p.value = 2 * stats::pnorm(abs(statistic), lower.tail = FALSE))
  }
  res %>%
    mutate(
      Model = label,
      raw_term = term,
      Term = paste0(clean_tactical_term(term), add_stars(p.value)),
      lower.OR = conf.low,
      upper.OR = conf.high
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(Model, term = raw_term, Term, OR = estimate, Statistic = statistic,
                  p.value, lower.OR, upper.OR)
}

mk_inv_contrasts <- function(mod, label) {
  contrast_df <- summary(
    contrast(
      emmeans(mod, ~ group),
      method = "trt.vs.ctrl",
      ref = "CC",
      adjust = "none"
    ),
    infer = TRUE,
    type = "response"
  ) %>%
    as_tibble()
  contrast_df_holm <- summary(
    contrast(
      emmeans(mod, ~ group),
      method = "trt.vs.ctrl",
      ref = "CC",
      adjust = "holm"
    ),
    infer = TRUE,
    type = "response"
  ) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    transmute(
      Contrast = gsub("\\s*/\\s*", " - ", contrast),
      p.value.holm = p.value
    )

  lower_col <- intersect(c("lower.CL", "asymp.LCL"), names(contrast_df))
  upper_col <- intersect(c("upper.CL", "asymp.UCL"), names(contrast_df))

  contrast_df %>%
    transmute(
      Model = label,
      Contrast = gsub("\\s*/\\s*", " - ", contrast),
      OR = odds.ratio,
      lower.OR = .data[[lower_col[1]]],
      upper.OR = .data[[upper_col[1]]],
      p.value = p.value
    ) %>%
    left_join(contrast_df_holm, by = "Contrast") %>%
    mutate(
      sig = p.value < 0.05,
      sig.holm = p.value.holm < 0.05,
      sensitivity_diff = sig != sig.holm
    )
}

tbl_resp <- mk_inv_glmm(resp_mod, "Responsiveness")
tbl_ret  <- mk_inv_glmm(ret_mod, "Retaliation")

investor_glmm_table <- bind_rows(tbl_resp, tbl_ret)
investor_glmm_contrasts <- bind_rows(
  mk_inv_contrasts(resp_mod, "Responsiveness"),
  mk_inv_contrasts(ret_mod, "Retaliation")
)

investor_glmm_print <- investor_glmm_table %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = c("Responsiveness", "Retaliation"))) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, Term, OR, Statistic, p.value, lower.OR, upper.OR) %>%
  dplyr::rename(`p-value` = p.value, `OR Low` = lower.OR, `OR High` = upper.OR) %>%
  mutate(
    OR = round(OR, 2),
    Statistic = round(Statistic, 2),
    `p-value` = signif(`p-value`, 3),
    `OR Low` = round(`OR Low`, 2),
    `OR High` = round(`OR High`, 2)
  )

apa_flex(investor_glmm_print,
         caption = "Trial-level hierarchical GLMMs for investor tactical responses",
         note = "* p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001")

## ---- Generate Supplement Table S5: Complete Investor GLMM Outputs ------
resp_summary <- summary(resp_mod)
ret_summary <- summary(ret_mod)

# Extract fixed effects for both models
resp_coef <- as.data.frame(coef(resp_summary))
resp_coef$Parameter <- rownames(resp_coef)
resp_coef$Model <- "Responsiveness"

ret_coef <- as.data.frame(coef(ret_summary))
ret_coef$Parameter <- rownames(ret_coef)
ret_coef$Model <- "Retaliation"

# Combine and format - using defensive list approach
inv_glmm_list <- list(resp_coef, ret_coef) %>% purrr::compact()
if (length(inv_glmm_list) > 0) {
  inv_glmm_full <- bind_rows(inv_glmm_list) %>%
    rename(SE = `Std. Error`, z = `z value`, p = `Pr(>|z|)`) %>%
    dplyr::select(Model, Parameter, Estimate, SE, z, p) %>%
    mutate(
      Estimate = sprintf("%.4f", Estimate),
      SE = sprintf("%.4f", SE),
      z = sprintf("%.2f", z),
      p = ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
    )

  # Save
  if (!dir.exists("supplement")) dir.create("supplement")
  write.csv(inv_glmm_full, "supplement/TableS5_Investor_GLMM_Complete.csv",
            row.names = FALSE)

} else {
}

options(contrasts = old_contrasts)
```

get_inv_contrast <- function(model_label, contrast_label) {
  row <- investor_glmm_contrasts %>%
    filter(Model == model_label, Contrast == contrast_label)
  if (nrow(row) == 0) {
    return(tibble::tibble(
      OR = NA_real_,
      lower.OR = NA_real_,
      upper.OR = NA_real_,
      p.value = NA_real_,
      p.value.holm = NA_real_,
      sensitivity_diff = FALSE
    ))
  }
  row
}

resp_bpd <- get_inv_contrast("Responsiveness", "BPD - CC")

    "< .001"
  } else {
    paste0("= ", format_pval(ret_effect$p.value))

} else {
