}
if (trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws != 10000L &&
    !identical(Sys.getenv("VTC_TRUSTEE_ALLOW_NONCANONICAL"), "1")) {
  stop("Noncanonical sensitivity draw counts are permitted only for smoke tests")
}

if (trustee_sensitivity_recompute) {
  trustee_sensitivity_output <- Sys.getenv(
    "VTC_TRUSTEE_SENSITIVITY_OUTPUT",
    file.path(
      "results", "HMM", "recomputed_from_analysis_main",
      sprintf(
        "state_count_sensitivity_B%d.rds",
        trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws
      )
    )
  )
  trustee_sensitivity_uses_canonical_result <- identical(
    normalizePath(trustee_sensitivity_output, mustWork = FALSE),
    normalizePath(trustee_sensitivity_canonical_path, mustWork = FALSE)
  )
  if (trustee_sensitivity_uses_canonical_result) {
    stop(paste(
      "Recomputation cannot overwrite the reviewed state-count",
      "sensitivity artifact; choose a separate",
      "VTC_TRUSTEE_SENSITIVITY_OUTPUT path"
    ))
  }
  trustee_sensitivity_state_counts <- c(4L, 6L)
  trustee_state_count_sensitivity <- purrr::map(
    trustee_sensitivity_state_counts,
    function(state_count) {
      trustee_run_state_count_sensitivity(
        model = trustee_search_result$selected_models[[
          as.character(state_count)
        ]]$ordered_group,
        data = trustee_dat %>% dplyr::arrange(subject_ID, round),
        bootstrap_draws = trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws,
        seed = 11L + state_count
      )
    }
  )
  names(trustee_state_count_sensitivity) <- as.character(
    trustee_sensitivity_state_counts
  )
  dir.create(
    dirname(trustee_sensitivity_output),
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = FALSE
  )
  saveRDS(trustee_state_count_sensitivity, trustee_sensitivity_output)
} else {
  stopifnot(
    file.exists(trustee_sensitivity_canonical_path),
    identical(
      digest::digest(
        file = trustee_sensitivity_canonical_path,
        algo = "sha256"
      ),
      trustee_sensitivity_expected_sha256
    )
  )
  trustee_state_count_sensitivity <- readRDS(
    trustee_sensitivity_canonical_path
  )
}

stopifnot(identical(names(trustee_state_count_sensitivity), c("4", "6")))

trustee_sensitivity_sampling_description <- if (trustee_sensitivity_recompute) {
  sprintf(
    paste(
      "Analyses with the neighbouring four- and six-state trustee models",
      "assessed sensitivity to state count, using %s successful bootstrap",
      "samples per model, with seeds 15 and 17, respectively."
    ),
    format(trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
  )
} else {
  paste(
    "Analyses with the neighbouring four- and six-state trustee models",
    "assessed sensitivity to state count, using 10,000 successful bootstrap",
    "samples per model. For each model, eight independently seeded batches",
    "of 1,250 samples were pooled before calculating confidence intervals",
    "and applying the original comparison-family corrections."
  )
}

for (state_count in as.integer(names(trustee_state_count_sensitivity))) {
  result <- trustee_state_count_sensitivity[[as.character(state_count)]]
  if (trustee_sensitivity_recompute) {
    stopifnot(identical(result$seed, 11L + state_count))
  } else {
    stopifnot(
      is.null(result$seed),
      identical(
        result$bootstrap_seeds,
        as.integer(11L + state_count + 1000L * (0:7))
      )
    )
  }
  selected_model <- trustee_search_result$selected_models[[
    as.character(state_count)
  ]]$ordered_group
  stopifnot(
    identical(result$state_count, state_count),
    identical(
      result$transition_orientation,
      "depmix_xi_to_from_transposed_to_from_to"
    ),
    identical(
      as.integer(result$bootstrap_status$successful_draws),
      trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws
    ),
    identical(
      as.integer(result$bootstrap_status$rejected_draws),
      0L
    ),
    nrow(result$point) == 36L,
    nrow(result$bootstrap$draws) ==
      trustee_sensitivity_expected_draws * 36L,
    nrow(result$state_dictionary) == state_count,
    identical(
      result$cooperative_states,
      result$state_dictionary$state[
        result$state_dictionary$broad_category == "cooperative"
      ]
    ),
    identical(
      result$exploitative_states,
      result$state_dictionary$state[
        result$state_dictionary$broad_category == "exploitative"
      ]
    ),
    identical(
      result$neutral_state,
      result$state_dictionary$state[
        result$state_dictionary$broad_category == "neutral"
      ]
    ),
    all(diff(result$state_dictionary$expected_return_fraction) > 0),
    nrow(result$cooperative_occupancy$summary) == 3L,
    nrow(result$cooperative_occupancy$pairs) == 3L,
    !anyDuplicated(
      result$bootstrap$draws[c(
        "iteration", "diagnosis", "investment", "metric"
      )]
    ),
    all(is.finite(result$bootstrap$draws$value)),
    all(
      result$bootstrap$draws$value >= 0 &
        result$bootstrap$draws$value <= 1
    ),
    identical(
      result$provenance$behavioral_data_sha256,
      digest::digest(
        file = file.path("Data", "full_RTG_data.csv"),
        algo = "sha256"
      )
    ),
    identical(
      result$provenance$model_parameter_sha256,
      digest::digest(getpars(selected_model), algo = "sha256")
    )
  )
}

trustee_sensitivity_state_dictionary <- dplyr::bind_rows(

for (state_count in as.integer(names(trustee_state_count_sensitivity))) {
  result <- trustee_state_count_sensitivity[[as.character(state_count)]]
  recalculated <- trustee_summarise_sensitivity_draws(
    result$bootstrap$draws,
    result$point %>% dplyr::select(-state_count)
  )
  saved_levels <- result$bootstrap$levels %>%
    dplyr::arrange(diagnosis, investment, metric)
  recalculated_levels <- recalculated$levels %>%
    dplyr::arrange(diagnosis, investment, metric)
  saved_contrasts <- result$bootstrap$contrasts %>%
    dplyr::arrange(investment, metric, contrast)
  recalculated_contrasts <- recalculated$contrasts %>%
    dplyr::arrange(investment, metric, contrast)
  stopifnot(
    isTRUE(all.equal(
      as.data.frame(saved_levels),
      as.data.frame(recalculated_levels),
      tolerance = 1e-12,
      check.attributes = FALSE
    )),
    isTRUE(all.equal(
      as.data.frame(saved_contrasts),
      as.data.frame(recalculated_contrasts),
      tolerance = 1e-12,
      check.attributes = FALSE
    ))
  )
}

trustee_orient_occupancy_contrast <- function(first_group, second_group) {
  direct_label <- paste(first_group, second_group, sep = " - ")
  reverse_label <- paste(second_group, first_group, sep = " - ")
  direct <- trustee_cooperative_occupancy_pairs %>%
    dplyr::filter(as.character(contrast) == direct_label)
  reverse <- trustee_cooperative_occupancy_pairs %>%
    dplyr::filter(as.character(contrast) == reverse_label)
  if (nrow(direct) == 1L && nrow(reverse) == 0L) {
    return(direct)
  }
  if (nrow(reverse) == 1L && nrow(direct) == 0L) {
    return(reverse %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        original_lower = lower,
        original_upper = upper,
        contrast = direct_label,
        difference = -difference,
        lower = -original_upper,
        upper = -original_lower
      ) %>%
      dplyr::select(-original_lower, -original_upper))
  }
  stop("Could not uniquely orient occupancy contrast ", direct_label)
}

    broom::tidy(stats::anova(model)) %>%
      dplyr::filter(term == "group") %>%
      dplyr::transmute(
        state = as.integer(state_number),

        F = statistic,
        p_raw = p.value

  dplyr::mutate(
    p_holm_across_states = stats::p.adjust(p_raw, method = "holm")

  trustee_state_occupancy_models,

    as.data.frame(summary(
      emmeans::contrast(
        emmeans::emmeans(model, ~group),
        method = "pairwise",
        adjust = "none"
      ),
      infer = c(TRUE, TRUE),
      adjust = "none"

      tibble::as_tibble() %>%
      dplyr::transmute(
        state = as.integer(state_number),
        contrast = as.character(contrast),
        difference = estimate,
        lower = lower.CL,
        upper = upper.CL,
        p_raw = p.value
      ) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        p_holm_within_state = stats::p.adjust(
          p_raw, method = "holm"
        ),
        correction_family = paste0(
          "3 group comparisons within State ", state_number
        )
      )
  }
)

  all(is.finite(trustee_state_occupancy_analysis_data$occupancy)),
  all(
    trustee_state_occupancy_analysis_data$occupancy >= 0 &
      trustee_state_occupancy_analysis_data$occupancy <= 1
  ),
  max(abs(
    trustee_state_occupancy_analysis_data %>%
      dplyr::group_by(subject_ID) %>%
      dplyr::summarise(total = sum(occupancy), .groups = "drop") %>%
      dplyr::pull(total) - 1
  )) < 1e-8,
  nrow(trustee_state_occupancy_omnibus) ==
    trustee_selected_state_count,
  nrow(trustee_state_occupancy_pairwise) ==
    trustee_selected_state_count * choose(
      nlevels(trustee_state_occupancy_analysis_data$group), 2L
    ),
  !anyDuplicated(trustee_state_occupancy_omnibus$state),
  !anyDuplicated(
    trustee_state_occupancy_pairwise[c("state", "contrast")]
  ),
  all(is.finite(
    unlist(trustee_state_occupancy_omnibus[c(
      "F", "p_raw", "p_holm_across_states"
    )])
  )),
  all(is.finite(
    unlist(trustee_state_occupancy_pairwise[c(
      "difference", "lower", "upper", "p_raw",
      "p_holm_within_state"
    )])
  )),
  all(
    trustee_state_occupancy_omnibus$p_holm_across_states + 1e-15 >=
      trustee_state_occupancy_omnibus$p_raw
  ),
  all(
    trustee_state_occupancy_pairwise$p_holm_within_state + 1e-15 >=
      trustee_state_occupancy_pairwise$p_raw
  ),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    trustee_state_occupancy_means %>%
      dplyr::arrange(group, state) %>%
      dplyr::pull(mean_occupancy),
    trustee_state_occupancy_summary %>%
      dplyr::arrange(group, state) %>%
      dplyr::pull(proportion),
    tolerance = 1e-12
  ))
)

# The saved intervals are Bonferroni-adjusted across three group contrasts,
# and the saved p values are Holm-adjusted. Recover standard errors from the
# unrounded intervals to display ordinary 95% confidence intervals and raw
# p values alongside the adjusted p values.
if (!"p_raw" %in% names(trustee_decoded_contrasts_table)) {
  bonferroni_critical_three <- stats::qnorm(
    1 - 0.05 / (2 * 3)
  )
  trustee_decoded_contrasts_table <-
    trustee_decoded_contrasts_table %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      standard_error = (
        log(upper_odds_ratio) - log(lower_odds_ratio)
      ) / (2 * bonferroni_critical_three),
      p_raw = 2 * stats::pnorm(
        -abs(log_odds_difference / standard_error)
      ),
      lower_odds_ratio = exp(
        log_odds_difference -
          stats::qnorm(0.975) * standard_error
      ),
      upper_odds_ratio = exp(
        log_odds_difference +
          stats::qnorm(0.975) * standard_error
      )
    )
}

  ) %>%

trustee_primary_level <- function(
    metric_name, diagnosis_name, investment_value) {
  row <- trustee_primary_levels_table %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      metric == metric_name,
      diagnosis == diagnosis_name,
      investment == investment_value
    )
  if (nrow(row) != 1L ||
      !all(is.finite(unlist(row[c(
        "point_estimate", "lower", "upper"
      )])))) {
    stop(
      "Could not find one finite primary level for ",
      metric_name, ", ", diagnosis_name, ", investment ",
      investment_value
    )
  }
  row
}

trustee_orient_transition_contrast <- function(
    table, metric_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value) {
  direct_label <- paste(first_group, second_group, sep = "-")
  reverse_label <- paste(second_group, first_group, sep = "-")
  direct <- table %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      metric == metric_name,
      as.character(contrast) == direct_label,
      investment == investment_value
    )
  reverse <- table %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      metric == metric_name,
      as.character(contrast) == reverse_label,
      investment == investment_value
    )
  if (nrow(direct) == 1L && nrow(reverse) == 0L) {
    row <- direct
  } else if (nrow(reverse) == 1L && nrow(direct) == 0L) {
    row <- reverse %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        original_lower = lower,
        original_upper = upper,
        contrast = direct_label,
        point_difference = -point_difference,
        lower = -original_upper,
        upper = -original_lower
      ) %>%
      dplyr::select(-original_lower, -original_upper)
  } else {
    stop(
      "Could not uniquely orient transition contrast ",
      direct_label, " for ", metric_name, " at investment ",
      investment_value
    )
  }
  required <- c(
    "point_difference", "lower", "upper", "p_two_sided",
    "p_holm_family"
  )
  if (!all(is.finite(unlist(row[required])))) {
    stop("Transition contrast contains non-finite values")
  }
  row
}

trustee_primary_contrast <- function(
    metric_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value) {
  trustee_orient_transition_contrast(
    trustee_primary_contrasts_table,
    metric_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value
  )
}

trustee_secondary_contrast <- function(
    metric_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value) {
  trustee_orient_transition_contrast(
    trustee_secondary_contrasts_table,
    metric_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value
  )
}

trustee_decoded_contrast <- function(
    event_name, first_group, second_group, investment_value) {
  direct_label <- paste(first_group, second_group, sep = " - ")
  reverse_label <- paste(second_group, first_group, sep = " - ")
  direct <- trustee_decoded_contrasts_table %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      event == event_name,
      contrast == direct_label,
      investment == investment_value
    )
  reverse <- trustee_decoded_contrasts_table %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      event == event_name,
      contrast == reverse_label,
      investment == investment_value
    )
  if (nrow(direct) == 1L && nrow(reverse) == 0L) {
    row <- direct
  } else if (nrow(reverse) == 1L && nrow(direct) == 0L) {
    row <- reverse %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        original_lower = lower_odds_ratio,
        original_upper = upper_odds_ratio,
        contrast = direct_label,
        log_odds_difference = -log_odds_difference,
        odds_ratio = 1 / odds_ratio,
        lower_odds_ratio = 1 / original_upper,
        upper_odds_ratio = 1 / original_lower
      ) %>%
      dplyr::select(-original_lower, -original_upper)
  } else {
    stop(
      "Could not uniquely orient decoded transition contrast ",
      direct_label, " for ", event_name, " at investment ",
      investment_value
    )
  }
  required <- c(
    "log_odds_difference", "odds_ratio", "lower_odds_ratio",
    "upper_odds_ratio", "p_holm_within_investment"
  )
  if (!all(is.finite(unlist(row[required])))) {
    stop("Decoded transition contrast contains non-finite values")
  }
  row
}

trustee_at_investment <- function(table, investment_value) {
  row <- table %>%
    dplyr::filter(investment == investment_value)
  if (nrow(row) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one row at investment ", investment_value)
  }
  row
}

For trustees, BIC selected `r trustee_selected_state_word` states within the group-dependent model family (Supplement Table S23). At this state count, allowing transitions to differ among diagnostic groups improved fit over the diagnosis-free model ($\chi^2$(`r trustee_five_state_likelihood_ratio$df[[1]]`) = `r scales::number(trustee_five_state_likelihood_ratio[["Likelihood-ratio statistic"]][[1]], accuracy = 0.01)`, *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_five_state_likelihood_ratio$p[[1]])`). Trials were assigned to states with moderate certainty: the mean probability of the most likely state was `r trustee_classification_certainty$mean_max_posterior_fmt`, and `r trustee_classification_certainty$share_confident_fmt` of trials were assigned with a probability of at least .80.















#### State Policies (Return Distributions)





The selected model recovered `r trustee_selected_state_word` ordered return profiles, with fitted mean returns of `r trustee_state_mean_text` of the tripled investment (Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-hmm-state-panel)A). State `r trustee_clearly_low_state` was classified as exploitative because its fitted mean return was substantially below one-third of the tripled investment. State `r trustee_break_even_state` was classified as neutral because the investor received approximately `r scales::number(trustee_break_even_receipt_ratio, accuracy = 0.01)` times the amount originally invested. States `r trustee_cooperative_range` were classified as cooperative because their fitted mean returns were clearly above one-third of the tripled investment. These descriptions refer to the economic consequences of the fitted return distributions rather than to trustees' intentions or psychological states.

```{r trustee-state-panel-caption, include=FALSE}
trustee_state_panel_caption <- paste0(
  "Trustee HMM state profiles and diagnostic occupancy. Panel A shows ",
  "emission distributions for the trustee HMM states; the x-axis gives ",
  "the proportion of the tripled endowment returned and the y-axis gives ",
  "the probability density under each latent state. Panel B shows, for ",
  "each diagnostic group, the proportion of trustee trials assigned to ",
  "each state in the most-likely-state analysis. States are ordered from ",
  "lower- to higher-return policies, so the combined figure links the ",
  "behavioural meaning of each latent state to where each diagnostic group ",
  "spent time along the cooperation continuum. Brackets and asterisks mark ",
  "pairwise group differences that remained significant after Holm ",
  "correction of the three comparisons within each state ",
  # Figure captions reach LaTeX as raw text and Word as markdown, so the
  # significance key is written once per format.
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    "(*** Holm-adjusted \\textit{p} < .001; ** \\textit{p} < .01; * \\textit{p} < .05)."
  } else {
    "(\\*\\*\\* Holm-adjusted *p* < .001; \\*\\* *p* < .01; \\* *p* < .05)."
  }
)
```

```{r trustee-hmm-state-panel, include=TRUE, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8, out.width='100%', fig.cap=trustee_state_panel_caption}
print(trustee_state_panel_plot)
```

We compared diagnostic groups in state occupancy and transition dynamics, analysing movements involving neutral State `r trustee_break_even_state` separately.

#### Transition Probabilities by Diagnostic Group







The complete fitted state-to-state transition functions for each diagnostic group are shown in Supplement Figure S1.

#### State Occupancy

















AD trustees had the highest cooperative-state occupancy in the most-likely-state analysis: `r scales::percent(trustee_cooperative_occupancy_mean("AD"), accuracy = 0.1)`, compared with `r scales::percent(trustee_cooperative_occupancy_mean("CC"), accuracy = 0.1)` for CC and `r scales::percent(trustee_cooperative_occupancy_mean("BPD"), accuracy = 0.1)` for BPD (Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-hmm-state-panel)B). Cooperative-state occupancy was `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_bpd$difference[[1]])` percentage points higher in AD than BPD (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_bpd$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_bpd$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_occupancy_ad_bpd$p_holm[[1]])`) and `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_cc$difference[[1]])` points higher in AD than CC (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_cc$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_ad_cc$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_occupancy_ad_cc$p_holm[[1]])`). The BPD–CC difference was not reliable (`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_bpd_cc$difference[[1]])` points, 95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_bpd_cc$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_occupancy_bpd_cc$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_occupancy_bpd_cc$p_holm[[1]])`).







State-specific comparisons showed that AD trustees occupied the exploitative State `r trustee_clearly_low_state` less often than BPD, by `r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_clearly_low_occupancy_ad_bpd$difference[[1]]))` percentage points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_clearly_low_occupancy_ad_bpd$upper[[1]]))`, `r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_clearly_low_occupancy_ad_bpd$lower[[1]]))`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_clearly_low_occupancy_ad_bpd$p_holm_within_state[[1]])`) and the neutral State `r trustee_break_even_state` by `r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_break_even_occupancy_ad_bpd$difference[[1]]))` points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_break_even_occupancy_ad_bpd$upper[[1]]))`, `r trustee_percentage_points(abs(trustee_break_even_occupancy_ad_bpd$lower[[1]]))`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_break_even_occupancy_ad_bpd$p_holm_within_state[[1]])`). AD also occupied State `r trustee_highest_return_state`, the highest-return state, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_cc$difference[[1]])` points more often than CC (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_cc$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_cc$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_cc$p_holm_within_state[[1]])`) and `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_bpd$difference[[1]])` points more often than BPD (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_bpd$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_bpd$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_highest_occupancy_ad_bpd$p_holm_within_state[[1]])`). Full state-specific results are reported in the Supplement. These findings indicate that AD trustees were less likely than BPD to occupy the exploitative and neutral states, and more likely than both BPD and CC to occupy the highest-return cooperative state.

#### Cooperation Dynamics

Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-contrast-panel) summarises the fitted probabilities of remaining cooperative, returning to cooperation after the exploitative State `r trustee_clearly_low_state`, leaving cooperation for that state, and occupying cooperative states in the long run if each partner-investment level continued across rounds. Complete estimates and group comparisons are reported in the Supplement.

```{r trustee-contrast-panel, include=TRUE, fig.width=13, fig.height=10, out.width='100%', fig.cap=trustee_primary_transition_caption}
print(trustee_primary_transition_plot)
```

**Cooperative retention.** Retention, defined as the probability of remaining in cooperative states from one round to the next, was lower in BPD than in CC at lower investment levels in both analyses, although statistical support was stronger in the most-likely-state analysis. In that analysis, the odds of remaining cooperative were `r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_5$odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)` times higher in CC than BPD at 5 tokens (95% CI [`r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_5$lower_odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)`, `r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_5$upper_odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_5$p_holm_within_investment[[1]])`) and `r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_10$odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)` times higher at 10 tokens (95% CI [`r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_10$lower_odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)`, `r scales::number(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_10$upper_odds_ratio[[1]], accuracy = 0.01)`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_decoded_retention_cc_bpd_10$p_holm_within_investment[[1]])`), with no reliable difference at 15 tokens. In the fitted transition model, retention at 5 tokens was `r scales::percent(trustee_retention_bpd_5$point_estimate[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in BPD and `r scales::percent(trustee_retention_cc_5$point_estimate[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in CC, a difference of `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_5$point_difference[[1]])` percentage points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_5$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_5$upper[[1]])`]; Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-contrast-panel)B), but this contrast did not remain significant after Holm adjustment (*p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_5$p_holm_family[[1]])`). At higher investments, this difference narrowed to `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_10$point_difference[[1]])` points at 10 tokens and `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_retention_bpd_cc_15$point_difference[[1]])` points at 15 tokens. No retention contrast in the fitted transition analysis remained significant after adjustment.

**Repair after exploitation.** Both analyses showed that AD trustees were more likely than BPD to return to cooperation after the exploitative State `r trustee_clearly_low_state` at all three investment levels. In the most-likely-state analysis, every AD–BPD comparison was significant (largest Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_decoded_repair_ad_bpd_p_max)`); CC trustees were also more likely than BPD to repair cooperation at 10 and 15 tokens (largest Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_decoded_repair_cc_bpd_10_15_p_max)`). In the fitted transition model, repair at 5 tokens was `r scales::percent(trustee_repair_ad_5$point_estimate[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in AD, `r scales::percent(trustee_repair_cc_5$point_estimate[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in CC, and `r scales::percent(trustee_repair_bpd_5$point_estimate[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in BPD. AD exceeded BPD by `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_bpd_5$point_difference[[1]])` percentage points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_bpd_5$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_bpd_5$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_repair_ad_bpd_5$p_holm_family[[1]])`) and CC by `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_cc_5$point_difference[[1]])` points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_cc_5$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_repair_ad_cc_5$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_repair_ad_cc_5$p_holm_family[[1]])`). The AD–BPD difference remained significant at 10 and 15 tokens, and BPD repair was lower than CC at both levels (largest Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_repair_followup_p_max)`; Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-contrast-panel)A).

Compared with CC, BPD trustees were less likely to return to cooperation from exploitative State `r trustee_clearly_low_state`; return from neutral State `r trustee_break_even_state` to cooperation did not differ reliably. AD trustees were more likely than CC to move from neutral State `r trustee_break_even_state` into cooperation at all three investment levels (largest Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_neutral_entry_ad_cc_p_max)`) and more likely than BPD at 10 and 15 tokens (largest Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_neutral_entry_ad_bpd_10_15_p_max)`; Supplement Tables S32–S33).

**Exploitative exits.** Neither analysis found reliable diagnostic-group differences in moves from cooperative States `r trustee_cooperative_range` to exploitative State `r trustee_clearly_low_state` (Figure \@ref(fig:trustee-contrast-panel)C).

**Model-implied long-run cooperation.** The fitted transition patterns implied greater long-run cooperation in AD if the same partner investment continued across rounds. AD exceeded BPD at every investment level, with the estimated difference increasing from `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_5$point_difference[[1]])` points at 5 tokens (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_5$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_5$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_5$p_holm_family[[1]])`) to `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_15$point_difference[[1]])` points at 15 tokens (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_15$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_15$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_stationary_ad_bpd_15$p_holm_family[[1]])`). AD also exceeded CC at 10 tokens by `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_10$point_difference[[1]])` points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_10$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_10$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_10$p_holm_family[[1]])`) and at 15 tokens by `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_15$point_difference[[1]])` points (95% CI [`r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_15$lower[[1]])`, `r trustee_percentage_points(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_15$upper[[1]])`], Holm-adjusted *p* `r format_pval_clause(trustee_stationary_ad_cc_15$p_holm_family[[1]])`). BPD–CC differences did not survive correction.

AD trustees repaired cooperation after exploitation more often and had greater model-implied long-run cooperation, particularly relative to BPD. AD–BPD differences in cooperative occupancy, repair, and model-implied long-run cooperation persisted among online trustees and after age and gender adjustment (Supplement Tables S17–S18 and S34). None of the long-run cooperation comparisons involving controls survived correction in these sensitivity analyses. BPD trustees showed lower cooperative retention than controls at smaller investments in the most-likely-state analysis and were less likely than controls to return to cooperation from the clearly exploitative state at medium and high investments in both analyses. Sensitivity analyses using four- and six-state models supported the AD–BPD differences in cooperative occupancy and model-implied long-run cooperation but showed that the BPD–CC retention and repair findings were sensitive to the number of states (Supplement).

















































# Discussion

This study used computational modelling to decompose trust and reciprocity in a large community and clinical sample including participants with BPD and an affective-symptom AD subgroup. By combining trial-level mixed-effects models with HMMs, we identified a clear dissociation between average behaviour and the dynamics through which cooperation unfolds. The trial-level analysis identified higher trustee returns in AD than in controls at the sample's average round and investment. Further differences emerged in how participants responded to their partners: first in round-by-round adjustment to the partner, and then in the maintenance and repair of cooperation across latent states. The findings differ in robustness. BPD was characterised by attenuated feedback-dependent adaptation in the investor role, alongside more model-dependent evidence of altered cooperative maintenance and repair in the trustee role. Among trustees, the most robust distinction was between the AD sample and BPD: AD trustees occupied cooperative states more often, repaired cooperation more readily, and showed higher model-implied long-run cooperation. This pattern broadly persisted across alternative state counts and in administration-mode and demographic checks. The BPD–CC trustee differences in maintenance and repair depended on the number of states and on whether transitions were taken from the fitted model or from most-likely-state sequences. The elevated AD tactical behaviours, and their interpretation as over-accommodation, remain provisional.

Maintenance and repair may index psychologically distinct interpersonal capacities rather than merely statistical decompositions of reciprocity. One psychological process that could contribute to maintenance is the capacity to sustain a flexible representation of the partner’s intentions in the face of ambiguous cues; repair may draw on the capacity to revise that representation after rupture and to recognise renewed cooperative intent rather than reading it as manipulation or irrelevance [@fonagy2017epistemic; @fonagy2009developmental]. We interpret these patterns through the lens of epistemic trust theory [@fonagy2017epistemic; @nolte2023epistemic; @lashani2026cracks], while noting that the specific mechanisms proposed were not directly measured in the present study. The same behavioural signatures are consistent with alternative accounts, including differential reinforcement sensitivity, loss aversion, and strategic sophistication. We develop the epistemic trust account in what follows because we believe it generates the most differentiated predictions for future work — specifically, measurable differences in mentalizing capacity, epistemic stance, and social learning that could be tested directly.

In the investor role, BPD was associated with significantly attenuated adaptation to partner returns. Investors with BPD were as likely as other participants to change the direction of their stakes after feedback, but adjusted magnitudes far less. The hidden-state analysis supported this pattern: BPD investors occupied the highest-investment state less often than CC, and greater net earnings shifted them less strongly towards higher-investment states. This dissociation between detection and use of social signals may be telling: partner feedback appears to be registered but not granted sufficient credibility to substantially revise expectations of the other person [@fonagy2017epistemic; @fonagy2015epistemic]. This is also consistent with evidence that individuals with BPD maintain more rigid self–other distinctions during social learning [@barnby2025selfother].

Among trustees, the clearest evidence concerned the AD sample. The strongest evidence was that AD trustees occupied cooperative states more often than BPD and showed greater cooperative repair and model-implied long-run cooperation across investment levels; AD also occupied the highest-return cooperative state more often than CC and showed higher model-implied long-run cooperation at medium and high investments. This was mirrored in the tactical analyses: encouragement was elevated relative to CC in the primary model, although this effect attenuated in both the demographic and administration-mode sensitivity analyses and should therefore be regarded as provisional. The AD–CC long-run cooperation differences in the primary model did not survive correction in the online and demographic sensitivity analyses. Rather, AD trustees, relative to BPD, returned to cooperation more readily after exploitative responses and had higher model-implied long-run cooperation, and in some contexts returned more when the investor reduced the stake. One hypothesis generated by this pattern is that elevated cooperative repair may in some individuals reflect compensatory interpersonal accommodation rather than more accurately calibrated social learning. The hypothesis draws on meta-analytic evidence that depression-related cooperation emerges specifically in paradigms where non-cooperation carries interpersonal cost [@jin2025depression], on the association between depression and guilt and submissive interpersonal tendencies [@oconnor2002guilt], and on the concept of epistemic credulity, an indiscriminate receptivity to social demands that manifests as compliance rather than calibrated responsiveness [@schwarzer2025epistemic]. Future studies combining the task with measures of guilt, submissiveness, and epistemic credulity could distinguish this account from genuinely enhanced cooperative responsiveness. The present data cannot adjudicate between these accounts, and the AD investor subgroup ($n = `r n_mdd_investors`$) was too small to test whether similar patterns appeared in both roles. The AD findings should therefore be treated as hypothesis-generating, with the encouragement result in particular requiring replication with fuller control for administration mode and demographic confounds.

The BPD–CC trustee pattern was less stable across model specifications. In the primary analysis, the BPD-related phenotype was a context-dependent fragility of cooperation. Retention in cooperative states was lower in BPD than CC at lower investments in the most-likely-state analysis, although the fitted transition estimates were less conclusive and the difference narrowed at higher investments. BPD trustees also showed context-dependent differences in returning to cooperation from the clearly exploitative state. Together with the absence of reliable evidence for increased exploitative exits, this pattern is most consistent with difficulty both sustaining cooperation when partner signals are weak and restoring it after an exploitative response, rather than with a global reduction in cooperative motivation. Low investment is not merely a smaller economic signal; it is a context in which the partner's intentions become harder to infer and therefore more vulnerable to hostile or rejecting interpretation [@staebler2011facial; @gunderson2011borderline]. Under conditions of unstable mentalizing, low investment may be read not as low generosity but as a socially meaningful sign of misattunement or impending abandonment — precisely the kind of ambiguous condition that places the greatest demands on flexible, controlled mentalizing [@fonagy2009developmental]. The instability in cooperative maintenance is therefore not random; it is elicited by the interactional conditions under which the partner's mind is hardest to read. Higher investment may stabilise the maintenance of cooperation by reducing this interpretive ambiguity. Emotion dysregulation [@linehan1993cognitive] may further accelerate transitions out of cooperative states once a negative reading has taken hold.

Notably, BPD trustees did not show reliable evidence of reduced coaxing. This is worth underscoring given the prominence of coaxing deficits in earlier accounts [@king-casas2008getting]. The absence of a coaxing difference argues against a general failure to emit repair signals. However, BPD trustees were less likely than CC to return to cooperation when their previous response was clearly exploitative at medium and high partner investments, whereas returning from the neutral state did not differ reliably. The results therefore suggest context-dependent differences in both maintenance and repair, rather than a difficulty confined to either process. The observed instability under low-stake conditions also resonates with the clinical phenomenology of rapid shifts in interpersonal stance: minor cues of ambiguous intent may precipitate an abrupt downgrading of the partner from potentially cooperative to insufficiently reliable [@skodol2002personality]. This parallel should be treated with caution, as the present data capture behavioural transitions rather than representational shifts, but it suggests a point of contact between this computational phenotype and the oscillation in representations of others that characterises BPD.

Because the investor and trustee roles were completed by different participants, any cross-role synthesis must remain conceptual. Nonetheless, the two findings may reflect distinguishable manifestations of altered epistemic calibration under uncertainty. In the trustee role, ambiguous low investment may be over-read as rejection and destabilise cooperative maintenance — a pattern compatible with epistemic hypervigilance, a defensive mode of intense scrutiny in which ambiguous cues are over-interpreted under conditions of expected interpersonal danger. In the investor role, partner feedback may be under-used as a basis for revising trust estimates — a pattern more consistent with epistemic mistrust in the narrower sense. Negative prior expectations are related but distinct: they would imply a more stable expectation that partners are unreliable across contexts, whereas hypervigilance and mistrust concern how ambiguous cues are interpreted and how feedback is used once encountered. Although related, these are not identical processes, and the present data cannot adjudicate between them directly.

Despite the marked differences in reciprocity dynamics, we detected no reliable group differences in payoffs. This does not establish equivalent social functioning. Behavioural differences need not translate into differences in total earnings: in repeated trust games with adaptive computer partners, participants scoring higher on self-serving personality traits returned less without obtaining significantly higher total payoffs [@guennouni2026price]. Earnings therefore need to be interpreted in light of how partners respond to participants' choices. If the clinically relevant dysfunction lies in the temporal organisation of interaction—processes that become unstable, brittle, and difficult to repair over time—then a short, constrained exchange may fail to reveal outcome differences even when the underlying cooperative dynamics differ substantially. The present design constrained precisely those processes that would ordinarily amplify the consequences of fragile cooperation. The nearest-neighbour algorithm could replay exploitative or generous human responses in locally similar situations, but it did not learn a participant-specific policy over repeated interaction. It therefore limited cumulative partner adaptation, such as progressively exploiting a consistently generous participant, retaliating against instability, or building increasing trust with a reliably cooperative one. The interpersonal costs of these patterns are likely to emerge in contexts involving reputation formation, memory for prior behaviour, and cumulative mutual adaptation — conditions that were deliberately minimised here.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study was not pre-registered; all analyses should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The present analyses were conducted on a fixed sample accumulated across parent studies rather than on a prospectively powered design. Because this manuscript analysed an already existing dataset, not all demographic variables requested by current reporting guidance were collected, including racial/ethnic identification, cultural or geographic background, and socioeconomic indicators; this limits assessment of sample representativeness along these dimensions. Participants were recruited from UK clinical and community settings; accordingly, the intended target populations are UK treatment-seeking patients with BPD and treatment-seeking affective-symptom service users, considered in relation to community participants recruited through the pathways described above. The findings should not be assumed to generalise to all people with BPD, depression, or anxiety, or to other national, cultural, and service contexts. The small AD investor subgroup therefore warrants particular caution. Second, the AD group combined depressive and anxiety presentations, limiting the specificity with which the observed pattern can be mapped onto any single affective-disorder mechanism. Third, medication status and comorbidity were not controlled, although both are common in these populations and may plausibly influence social decision-making. Fourth, administration mode (remote vs. in-person) was unevenly distributed across diagnostic groups, as the protocol shifted to remote administration partway through recruitment. Supplementary sensitivity analyses controlling for mode showed that the primary LMM effects (BPD attenuated investor adaptation and AD elevated trustee returns) were robust, but the AD encouragement tactical effect attenuated to non-significance, consistent with the demographic sensitivity results. Fifth, the computerised partner design afforded experimental control but limited participant-specific reputation formation and cumulative mutual adaptation. Participants also believed they were interacting with humans, which raises the question of whether behaviour would have differed had the artificial nature of the partner been known. The findings therefore describe responses to controlled social signals rather than the full dynamics of relationships in which both partners learn and adapt. Finally, the HMM transition intervals reported here are conditional on the selected state structure and fixed emission model, and so do not propagate full uncertainty over state number or emission specification. Sensitivity analyses showed that some conclusions were more stable than others. The AD–BPD differences in cooperative-state occupancy and model-implied long-run cooperation persisted in the four- and six-state models, whereas the precise BPD–CC pattern of retention and repair varied with the number of states. This supports the broader AD–BPD difference in reciprocity dynamics but requires caution in treating the balance between maintenance and repair in BPD relative to CC as definitive. The psychological validity of the recovered HMM states nonetheless remains to be established more directly, for example through associations with measures of mentalizing such as reflective functioning, of epistemic trust, mistrust, and credulity, and of rejection sensitivity, and with symptom severity. Future work should seek to replicate these findings in pre-registered studies with more balanced samples, finer-grained characterisation of affective symptoms, fuller assessment of medication and comorbidity, tests of association with symptom severity, and interactions involving either live partners or adaptive agents capable of learning individual behavioural patterns.

One way to test the role of ambiguous partner signals is to manipulate the information available about the partner. In a repeated trust-game experiment, displaying emotion cues linked to a computer investor's underlying response pattern increased trustee returns, with effects depending on presentation order [@guennouni2024cues]. A clinical follow-up could compare visible and concealed cues while holding the partner's response rules constant, and measure participants' interpretations of the partner's intentions alongside their choices. This would test whether clearer partner signals alter cooperation and whether changes in interpretation accompany changes in behaviour.

## Clinical Implications

These computational phenotypes may have preliminary translational relevance, although any clinical implications remain provisional and require replication. If the pattern of over-accommodating prosocial responding in this AD sample proves robust, affected individuals may be especially vulnerable to exploitation in unstructured relationships, even if those risks are not readily apparent in standardised therapeutic or experimental contexts. This vulnerability may be compounded if the over-accommodation observed here reflects epistemic credulity — a reduced capacity to discriminate between social demands that warrant compliance and those that do not [@schwarzer2025epistemic] — a pattern that has been linked to depressive presentations in particular and may therefore apply most strongly to the depressive component of this mixed sample. Interventions might then focus on helping patients identify trigger contexts, particularly partner hesitation or reduced investment, and legitimising proportional rather than compensatory reciprocity, in line with work identifying guilt and submissive responding as clinically salient in depression [@oconnor2002guilt; @gotlib2010cognition]. For BPD, if fragile cooperation proves replicable, MBT approaches [@bateman2004mentalization; @fonagy2015epistemic] may be well placed to address two role-specific challenges suggested by the present data: in the trustee role, interpreting ambiguous partner signals without over-inferring rejection; and in the investor role, updating models of the partner progressively on the basis of accumulating evidence. One potential therapeutic target suggested by these findings, pending replication, is helping patients recognise and use renewed cooperative signals from others, rather than focusing exclusively on signalling their own cooperative intent. The differential pattern across groups also suggests that intervention may need to be tailored, with guilt-focused work potentially more relevant for AD and epistemic-trust-oriented work more relevant for BPD [@nolte2023epistemic], although symptom-level correlates remain to be established. Experimental evidence suggests that responses to a withdrawal of trust can be modified: a brief cognitive intervention increased trustee returns and reduced retaliation following a programmed low investment in non-clinical adults [@guennouni2025rebuilding]. Whether comparable changes occur in clinical populations remains to be tested. Computational measures derived from Trust Games may eventually complement conventional symptom assessments by providing quantitative indicators of social functioning that are sensitive to treatment-related change [@huys2015computational].

## Conclusion

In conclusion, diagnostic groups differed in how they adjusted trust and maintained or restored cooperation across repeated social exchange. BPD was most consistently characterised by attenuated adjustment of investment following partner feedback, whereas the trustee analyses indicated more context- and model-dependent differences in cooperative maintenance and repair. The most robust trustee distinction was between BPD and the affective-symptom sample, which showed greater cooperative-state occupancy, repair, and model-implied long-run cooperation. These dynamic phenotypes are candidate behavioural markers of altered social learning and interpersonal adaptation. The proposed links to mentalizing, epistemic stance, rejection sensitivity, and interpersonal accommodation remain interpretations of the behavioural pattern that require direct measurement in future studies.
